docs.title: Develop a RAG technique and test it inside a full pipeline.
docs.text:
Lasagna splits a retrieval-augmented generation pipeline into eight stages. You swap one component, hold the other seven fixed, and get a verdict on whether the difference is real. The same pipeline also serves your agent over MCP and REST.

Get started Compare a component View on GitHub Project page and paper

docs.title: Why it exists
docs.text:
RAG papers report one component at a time. A new reranker is measured against a baseline with no query expansion and an old chunker. If a reranker claims +4 NDCG and a query expander claims +3, you cannot tell from the papers whether stacking them gives +7, +4 or -1.

The study behind Lasagna tested 450 configurations across eight benchmarks. The three strongest single retrieval techniques were predicted to add 47% NDCG@10 together. They added 17%. Faithfulness gains did carry over. The paper study has the detail.

8swappable pipeline stages

55built-in components

31public benchmarks

0API keys for a retrieval comparison

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install lasagna-rag
python -m nltk.downloader punkt_tab

Lasagna runs on Python 3.10 to 3.13. The speed profile downloads one 92 MB model and never calls an LLM. See installation for extras and platform notes.

docs.title: Your first comparison
docs.text:
Put a reranker in my_ideas.py:

import lasagna

@lasagna.reranker
def keyword_overlap(query, text):
    return len(set(query.lower().split()) & set(text.lower().split()))

Save a sweep as sweep.yaml. It runs your reranker against a built-in one, with everything else fixed:

name: does keyword_overlap help
benchmarks: [{name: smoke}]
tracks: [retrieval]
pipeline:
  base_profile: speed
  rerankers: [cross_encoder, "my_ideas:keyword_overlap"]
n_runs: 1

Run it, then ask whether the gap is real:

lasagna benchmark experiment sweep.yaml
lasagna results significance results.json --all

Your first comparison walks through the output, and shows the same sweep on a real benchmark.

docs.title: What it reproduces
docs.text: On the full SciFact and NFCorpus test sets, the built-in dense models land within 0.002 NDCG@10 of their MTEB results. BM25 followed by a MiniLM cross-encoder lands within 0.004 of the BEIR paper. Nothing was tuned. The reproduction guide shows the table and the command.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Which settings are in force, where Lasagna keeps its data, and which LLM it calls. Every setting, with its type, default and environment variable, is in the settings reference, which is generated from the code.

To see what applies to a session right now:

lasagna doctor -s my-corpus      # session, profile, settings file and data directory in force

docs.title: Where a setting comes from
docs.text:
A setting is looked up in this order, and the first place that has it wins:

Order Source Set by Scope 1 Per-query overrides the evaluation harness, for each arm of a sweep one query 2 Session overrides lasagna configure, lasagna import, lasagna init, the REST config routes, the MCP config tools, the configurator page one session 3 Environment variables LASAGNA_<NAME> or RAG_<NAME> the process 4 The settings file the packaged settings.lasagna.toml, or the file LASAGNA_SETTINGS_FILE (or RAG_SETTINGS_FILE) names the process 5 Built-in defaults the code the process

So the settings file and the environment set the defaults for a process, and the session overrides that lasagna configure writes win for that session. lasagna configure --profile speed -s A changes session A only; another session, and a new one, still start from the settings file and the environment. A profile sets only the settings that define it (for speed, the MiniLM model, no reranking and the rest of its list); the vector backend and every other setting it does not name still come from the environment and the settings file.

What a session can set. Session overrides hold retrieval and generation settings: the ones that reach a pipeline stage (chunking, embedding model, retrieval, query enhancement, reranking, agentic retrieval, generation) and how results are cited. Where data lives and how the server reaches it (the vector backend and its connection settings, the collection, index settings, paths, URLs, credentials, limits) are the process's, from the environment and the settings file. Every surface that writes session overrides refuses those keys, and keys that are no setting, with an error naming each one; a value equal to the one already in force is dropped instead, so an exported configuration imports again. A model named by a path or URL is refused the same way.

Where session overrides are kept. In the metadata database (SQLite under the data directory, or PostgreSQL when database_backend is postgresql), for every surface: the lasagna command, lasagna-mcp, lasagna serve and Python code. A profile set by one command applies in the next one, in a running server and in a KnowledgeClient for that session; the compose stack's api workers, Celery worker and MCP server read one session's settings alike. RAG_SESSION_BACKEND=memory keeps a process's sessions in memory, for the life of the process (tests, or a notebook that should leave saved sessions alone).

From Python, a KnowledgeConfig passed to KnowledgeClient splits the same way: the fields that choose what the process connects to (vector backend, database, cache) are written where environment variables go, before the backend starts, and apply to the whole process; the search and chunking fields become session overrides for the client's session. The embedding model is both: the process's default, and the client's session setting, which wins, so each session indexes and searches with its own model and two clients in one process on different sessions can use different models. The SDK configuration page lists which is which.

Environment variables. Every setting reads from LASAGNA_<NAME> and from RAG_<NAME>, in capitals (LASAGNA_CHUNK_SIZE=512). When both are set, the LASAGNA_ one wins. A value that does not parse, is out of range or is not one of the allowed values stops the process with an error naming the variable, its value and what it takes. A RAG_ name that is no setting prints one warning with the closest setting. An empty value counts as unset. on, off, yes, no, 1 and 0 are booleans.

The log level is the log_level setting, LASAGNA_LOG_LEVEL or RAG_LOG_LEVEL: the console level of the lasagna command (WARNING unless set), the MCP server and the REST server. A value it does not take warns and is ignored, so a typo never stops lasagna doctor.

A few LASAGNA_ variables are not settings: LASAGNA_DATA_DIR, LASAGNA_DB_DIR and LASAGNA_UPLOAD_DIR (below), LASAGNA_SETTINGS_FILE, LASAGNA_LOG_FORMAT=json, LASAGNA_MCP_TOOLS, LASAGNA_LLM_CACHE=0 (turns the experiment cache off) and LASAGNA_STRICT_PLUGINS=1.

.env files. Lasagna does not load .env into the environment. The one exception: the lasagna command reads RAG_SETTINGS_FILE from ./.env in the working directory when the variable is not already set, because that is where lasagna init records the settings file it wrote. Python code, other directories and lasagna-mcp do not; there, export RAG_SETTINGS_FILE=... first. API keys are never read from .env: export them in your shell.

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text:
A profile is a set of session overrides with a name. lasagna configure lists them and lasagna configure --profile NAME -s SESSION applies one. There are five: default, which is the settings file as it stands, and four presets.

Profile What it runs Downloads on first use Calls an LLM during search default the settings file: BGE-M3, hierarchical chunking, hybrid search, reranking with mxbai-rerank-large-v1, MMR, query routing with agentic retrieval 3.2 GB for queries routed to agentic retrieval speed dense vector search only, all-MiniLM-L6-v2; no reranking, hybrid, MMR, HyDE or agentic loop 92 MB never standard hybrid search, reranking with mxbai-rerank-large-v1, MMR, query routing with agentic retrieval, BGE-M3 3.2 GB for queries routed to agentic retrieval balanced standard plus hierarchical chunking, the structured agentic graph with a hallucination check, and adaptive routing 3.2 GB for queries routed to agentic retrieval max_quality balanced plus HyDE, query expansion, RAG fusion, CRAG, an answer quality check and contextual retrieval (an LLM call per chunk at ingest); every query goes to the agentic loop 3.2 GB on every search and every upload

The sizes are the model weights, which lasagna init also prints. With query routing on, each query is classified by rules: a short factual one runs vector search only, most run the profile's pipeline, and one judged complex goes to the agentic loop, which calls an LLM. Without an API key such a query runs the profile's pipeline instead, and the result names agentic in degraded_stages; the MCP search tool does the same for a session that sends every query to the agentic loop. speed is the profile that never calls an LLM and downloads no large model. A benchmark run picks its profile with lasagna benchmark run --profile, or base_profile: in a sweep file. lasagna benchmark run starts from speed unless told otherwise, and a sweep file without base_profile: starts from standard; --dry-run and the run header print the profile each arm starts from.

docs.title: Where data lives
docs.text:
Everything a user stores is under one data directory, ~/.lasagna: the metadata database and the Milvus Lite store in dbs/, uploaded files in uploads/, experiment results in research/results/ (for a sweep without output_dir:), and the experiment LLM cache in cache/llm.sqlite.

Variable Default What it places LASAGNA_DATA_DIR (or RAG_DATA_DIR) ~/.lasagna the whole data directory LASAGNA_DB_DIR (or RAG_DB_DIR) <data dir>/dbs the metadata database and the Milvus Lite store LASAGNA_UPLOAD_DIR (or RAG_UPLOAD_DIR) <data dir>/uploads uploaded files

LASAGNA_DATA_DIR moves the results and the cache with the rest; llm_cache: {path: ...} in a sweep puts the cache file elsewhere.

Milvus Lite admits one process per store. When another process holds the default one (a running lasagna serve, an MCP server, or another benchmark), lasagna benchmark run and lasagna benchmark experiment use a store of their own in <data dir>/bench/dbs and say so. Benchmark corpora are ingested there once and reused by later runs that find the default store held; a run that finds it free uses dbs/ as before. A store chosen with LASAGNA_DB_DIR or a db_path is never moved: the run stops before it starts and says what to do. An experiment started from Python stops the same way.

Before 0.1.0 the data directory was ~/.rag_knowledge. The first time the default is used and only ~/.rag_knowledge exists, it is renamed to ~/.lasagna. When both exist nothing is moved or deleted, and a warning gives the mv command, or LASAGNA_DATA_DIR=~/.rag_knowledge to keep using the old one.

The metadata store records its version. SQLite and PostgreSQL stores keep a store version, and a Lasagna that finds a store written by a newer version refuses to open it, naming both versions. Upgrade the package, or point LASAGNA_DB_DIR (or the PostgreSQL DSN) at another store. Downgrading over a store is therefore not possible. The deployment guide covers upgrading a running stack.

docs.title: One collection per embedding model
docs.text:
Vectors from two embedding models cannot be compared, even at the same size (BAAI/bge-large-en-v1.5 and BAAI/bge-m3 both produce 1024 dimensions). So each model writes to a collection of its own, named rag_documents_v2__<model>__<dimensions>, for example rag_documents_v2__all_minilm_l6_v2__384 for the speed profile.

  • Setting embedding_model without embedding_dim (in the environment, a session or KnowledgeConfig) uses that model's own size, read from a table of common models or from the model's files in the Hugging Face cache. When neither has it, an upload is refused before anything is stored, naming the setting to add.
  • Sessions on the same model share its collection, and each session sees only its own documents in it.
  • Switching a session to a profile with another model makes it search that model's collection, so a session that holds documents is refused the switch, even at the same embedding size: none of its documents would be found. Use a new session for the new model, or switch and reindex in one step: lasagna configure --profile <name> -s <session> --reindex (reindex=true on PUT /api/v1/config/profiles/{name} and PUT /api/config/knowledge/active, and on the MCP tool set_active_profile). It first checks that the new profile's models load (downloaded, or downloadable here), then reindexes every document with the new profile while the session stays on the old one, and switches only once all of them are reindexed. If one fails, the documents already moved are moved back, the session keeps its profile, and the error names the document and why. While it runs, an upload, reindex, delete or settings change of that session from anywhere else is refused (409 over REST) and a second switch waits for it; stopped part way (Ctrl-C), it moves the documents back first. One whose process died is reported by lasagna doctor -s <session> and finished by lasagna configure --resume-switch -s <session>. lasagna doctor -s <session> also reports documents that sit in another model's collection as blocking. To switch without moving them, use lasagna configure --profile <name> -s <session> --force (force=true over REST and MCP), which also checks that the new models load, and reindex the documents with the new model afterwards: client.documents.reindex(document_id) in the SDK, POST /api/v1/documents/{id}/reindex (or POST /api/knowledge/reindex for all of a session's documents) over REST, or the MCP tool reindex_document. A reindex moves each document to the new model's collection and keeps answering from the old one until the new chunks are stored; one that fails leaves the document as it was. Until then the documents stay where they were, and a session on the old model still finds them. Uploading a file again also indexes it for the new model: an upload is a duplicate only of a copy in the collection the session searches now.
  • A session's own settings (written by an SDK client, a patch or an import) stay in force across a switch. lasagna configure --reset -s <session> drops them, so the profile's settings apply as they are; with --profile it switches as well, and --force and --reindex work as above (reset=true on PUT /api/config/knowledge/active). In Python these refusals are KnowledgeErrors you can import: from lasagna.sdk import DocumentsLeftBehind, ProfileCannotLoad, ReindexFailed (with EmbeddingSizeConflict, ProfileSwitchInProgress, UnknownProfileError, and SettingsNotSaved when the metadata store did not record a change: then nothing changed, and REST answers 503).
  • A collection_name you set yourself (in the settings file or as RAG_COLLECTION_NAME) is used as given. The evaluation harness names one per sweep arm this way, so sweeps are unaffected.
  • Each collection records the model and size it was created with. Opening it with another model is refused with a message naming both models and the command that switches back, and nothing is changed.

A store from before 0.1.0 has one collection, rag_documents_v2, shared by every model, and nothing recorded which model wrote it. Name that model with LASAGNA_LEGACY_COLLECTION_MODEL (for example BAAI/bge-m3), and that model keeps using the collection under its old name; any other model gets its own. Until then a model of the same size logs a warning saying so, and lasagna status lists the collection.

docs.title: LLM providers and models
docs.text:
With no LLM configured, Lasagna uses the first of these API keys it finds in the environment, in this order, with that provider's default model:

Provider Key Default model OpenAI OPENAI_API_KEY gpt-6-luna Anthropic ANTHROPIC_API_KEY claude-sonnet-5-5 Groq GROQ_API_KEY openai/gpt-oss-120b Mistral MISTRAL_API_KEY mistral-large-latest Together TOGETHER_API_KEY meta-models/Muse-Glimmer-30B DeepSeek DEEPSEEK_API_KEY deepseek-flash Google GOOGLE_API_KEY gemini-3.6-flash Azure OpenAI AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY gpt-5.6-luna (a deployment name) OpenRouter OPENROUTER_API_KEY anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5 Fireworks FIREWORKS_API_KEY accounts/fireworks/models/llama-v3p1-70b-instruct Cohere COHERE_API_KEY command-a-03-2025 NVIDIA NVIDIA_API_KEY meta/llama-3.1-70b-instruct Perplexity PERPLEXITY_API_KEY sonar watsonx WATSONX_APIKEY (or WATSONX_API_KEY) meta-llama/llama-4-maverick-17b-128e-instruct-fp8 Ollama OLLAMA_BASE_URL llama3.2 vLLM VLLM_BASE_URL the model the server loaded llama.cpp LLAMACPP_MODEL_PATH the file it names Hugging Face (local) HF_MODEL_ID the model it names

MODEL_NAME picks another model on that provider. The core install talks to OpenAI, Azure OpenAI and every OpenAI-compatible endpoint (Together, DeepSeek, OpenRouter, Fireworks, Perplexity, Ollama, vLLM). Anthropic, Google, Mistral, Cohere and NVIDIA need the providers extra (pip install "lasagna-rag[providers]"), a local Hugging Face model needs the local extra, and Groq, watsonx and llama.cpp need their LangChain package (langchain-groq, langchain-ibm, langchain-community with llama-cpp-python), which no extra installs. Writing your own provider, or configuring one in code, is covered in the providers package.

In an experiment, the answers come from RAG_EVAL_GENERATOR_MODEL, else MODEL_NAME, else the provider default above. The judge is separate: RAG_EVAL_JUDGE_MODEL, else judge_model: in the sweep file, else gpt-6-luna. The run metadata and the comparability key name the judge, so results judged by different models never share a leaderboard group.

docs.title: Temperature and repeatable runs
docs.text:
Lasagna asks for temperature 0 wherever it wants a repeatable answer, and builds each request for the model it goes to, because current models do not all accept a temperature:

Model What is sent Claude 4.7 and later (claude-sonnet-5-5, claude-haiku-5-5, ...) no temperature, top_p or top_k; the API refuses them Claude 4.6 and earlier temperature as asked OpenAI reasoning models that allow it (gpt-6-luna, gpt-6-sol, gpt-5.6-luna, ...) reasoning_effort: "none" with the temperature OpenAI reasoning models that do not (gpt-6-astra, gpt-6.1-sol, gpt-5) no temperature Any other model temperature as asked

Setting reasoning_effort in the model settings to anything but "none" means no temperature is sent. The RAGAS judge's requests are built the same way, at the 0.01 RAGAS asks for.

A model that is sent no temperature answers differently from run to run, and Lasagna says so rather than claim otherwise: lasagna doctor and the start of an experiment print one line naming the model, the run metadata records sampling: provider-default for the generator or the judge, and the experiment cache never replays its answers. Repeat runs (n_runs: 3 or more) to measure that spread. Retrieval with fixed models does not sample, so a retrieval-only sweep needs one run.

docs.title: Contributing a component
docs.text:
How a researcher gets from an idea to a published, checkable result, and what makes each step auditable rather than just easy.

The design goal is narrow: it should be hard to produce a number you cannot defend. Everything below follows from that.

docs.title: The path, end to end
docs.text:
Five steps. Each is one command, and each is a checkpoint that can fail.

# Step Command What it rules out 1 Write it one decorator on a function 2 Check the contract lasagna component validate my_ideas:keyword_overlap it does not satisfy its stage's contract (types, top_k, empty input, no mutation of its input) 3 Check it runs lasagna benchmark run smoke --reranker my_ideas:keyword_overlap --profile speed it breaks inside the pipeline 4 Check it helps lasagna benchmark experiment sweep.yaml the gain is noise, or was never measured 5 Publish lasagna results bundle, then validate nobody can tell what produced the number

The ordering is the design. Every step catches a failure the next one would otherwise disguise as a result.

docs.title: 1. Write it
docs.text:
One decorator on a plain function. Put this in my_ideas.py:

import lasagna


@lasagna.reranker(
    "keyword_overlap", paper="Someone et al. 2026", claims={"beir/scifact": {"ndcg@10": 0.42}}
)
def keyword_overlap(query, text):
    """Count the query words that appear in the passage."""
    return len(set(query.lower().split()) & set(text.lower().split()))

The decorator wraps the function in the stage's interface (BaseReranker) and registers it. The wrapper hands the function copies of what it receives, so it cannot change what another stage sees. Each stage takes the natural signature:

Stage Function reranker f(query, text) -> float, or f(query, documents, top_k) -> documents query_enhancer f(query) -> list[str] chunker f(text) -> list[str] embedder f(texts) -> one vector per text retriever f(query, top_k) -> list[str] or documents document_processor f(file_path) -> str generator f(query, contexts) -> str (the answer)

The agentic pipeline is the one stage with no one-line form: a loop is a class (below).

paper and claims are optional and worth filling in: they come back out of the registry, a run records them, and on a run of the benchmark a claim names, its leaderboards and results view show the claimed number beside the one you reproduced. That comparison is the most useful thing a reader of your result can see. A claim is keyed by benchmark, {"beir/scifact": {"ndcg@10": 0.42}}, with "split": "test" inside if the paper names a split; a claim that names no benchmark is refused, since it would print beside a run of any benchmark.

A technique with state or a model is a class instead: subclass the stage's interface (BaseReranker and so on), register it with @registry.register("reranker", "name"), and deep-copy its inputs before changing them.

docs.title: 2. Check the contract
docs.text:
lasagna component validate my_ideas:keyword_overlap

It imports from the working directory, as a sweep does. A function registered with @lasagna.<stage> is checked as the wrapper a sweep would run; a plain, undecorated function needs --stage <stage>; a class is named the same way, my_package.reranker:MyReranker.

Registration and conformance are different things, and the difference is load-bearing. A component can register successfully and still not satisfy its ABC; it is then listed with implements_contract: False, and comparing against it measures the interface difference along with the algorithm.

[r["name"] for r in registry.list_rerankers() if r["implements_contract"]]

That list is the set of fair baselines. Use it.

docs.title: What validation does not prove
docs.text:
It exercises the component in isolation. That is deliberate (it is the fastest possible check), but it means a green result does not mean the pipeline can call your component. A wrapper bridges the orchestrator's internal reranker signature to BaseReranker (it passes query, documents and top_k); if such a bridge broke, a component would fail the first time it ran for real, after every isolated check passed.

Which is why step 3 exists and is not optional.

docs.title: 3. Check it runs
docs.text:
lasagna benchmark run smoke --reranker my_ideas:keyword_overlap --profile speed

24 documents, 12 queries, held inside the package. No dataset download, no API key. It runs the real pipeline end to end with your component in its stage, so a green run means your component is wired in. my_ideas:keyword_overlap is an import path: the CLI imports it from the working directory, so the function needs no package. Installed plugins are named by their registered name. --query-enhancer and --generator name a component of those stages the same way.

It is deliberately easy. The score means "this works", never "this is good".

docs.title: 4. Check it helps
docs.text:
This is the step the whole exercise is for, and the one where numbers most often go wrong.

# sweep.yaml
name: does my reranker help
benchmarks:
  - name: beir/scifact
    n_samples: 100
tracks: [retrieval]                                 # no LLM or RAGAS needed
pipeline:
  base_profile: speed                               # no LLM key, small models
  rerankers: [cross_encoder, "my_ideas:keyword_overlap"]   # a control and yours
n_runs: 1                                           # retrieval does not sample

lasagna benchmark experiment sweep.yaml
lasagna results significance "<output>/results.json" -m ndcg@10 --all

Every listed built-in implements its stage's interface, so cross_encoder is a like-for-like control. Naming a reranker turns reranking on for that arm, even on speed. Before ingesting anything the run checks that each named component passes its stage's contract, and when it finishes it confirms that the configuration reaching each stage differed only at the reranker (or says which other stage moved), and flags your arm as inert if its ranked lists never moved. The second command prints each pair with the difference, the effect size and both the raw and the Holm-adjusted p. For keyword_overlap (query words found in the passage) against the cross-encoder on 100 SciFact queries, a real run printed:

pair                                     diff    d_z        p  p (Holm)    n
reranker=cross_encoder                +0.0913  +0.38  1.0e-04   1.0e-04  100  significant
vs reranker=my_ideas:keyword_overlap

╭─ significant after Holm correction ─────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ reranker=cross_encoder beats reranker=my_ideas:keyword_overlap              │
│   ndcg@10 +0.0913 on beir/scifact, d_z +0.38, p (Holm) 1.0e-04, 100 queries │
│                                                                             │
│ 1 of 1 pair survives correction at family-wise alpha=0.05.                  │
╰─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

The box at the end says what the table supports. Green names each pair that survives the correction, which side won and by how much. When nothing survives, a yellow box says so and points at lasagna results power, which tells "the arms perform alike" apart from "too few queries to tell".

Three things this enforces that a hand-rolled comparison does not:

A control arm. Without one you cannot distinguish "my component reordered things" from "my component never ran". The two look identical from outside.

Everything else held fixed. Same chunker, same embedder, same top-k, same split, same sample. The difference is attributable because nothing else moved.

A paired test over queries. Per-sample scores are carried through and paired by sample identity, so the test compares the two arms on the same queries. Retrieval with fixed models returns the same lists on every run, so one run is enough; repeat runs when an LLM stage is in the loop (an LLM reranker, HyDE, an agentic pipeline, answer generation), where answers vary from run to run.

Other stages sweep the same way. chunkers:, embedders:, query_enhancers: and generators: take lists like rerankers:. A chunker or embedder arm gets a corpus of its own, chunked or embedded by its component (an embedder also gets its own collection), so arms never share an index. A retriever or an agentic pipeline is named in a config_overrides entry, such as {name: bm25, retriever: bm25}, with dense as the retriever control. Document processors do not sweep, since benchmark corpora are loaded as text. The guide, section 8 has a retriever sweep and a generator sweep.

Component overrides only apply in live mode. generation_only never constructs the pipeline, so passing a component there is a hard error rather than a plausible number scored against gold context. mode: auto picks correctly and logs which it chose and why.

docs.title: 5. Publish
docs.text:
lasagna results bundle results.json -o run.json
lasagna results validate run.json

--strict also fails on integrity warnings that do not block a local run, such as SINGLE_RUN (raised only when something in the run samples, so the retrieval-only n_runs: 1 above passes) and UNRESOLVED_JUDGE_ALIAS; lasagna results view results.json writes the whole run as one HTML page to attach to a review, and lasagna results leaderboard <dir> --format latex prints a table for a paper.

The bundle carries library versions, hardware, the resolved sweep, the corpus fingerprint, the sample-id digest, and a comparability key: a hash over everything held fixed, deliberately excluding the dimension under test.

That exclusion is the whole design. A key covering everything would make every row incomparable with every other; a key covering nothing would make all rows comparable regardless of what they measured.

Submit to the results hub as a pull request adding one file.

docs.title: What makes this auditable
docs.text:
Four properties, each mechanical rather than social.

A naive edit is caught. run_id hashes the bundle contents and the comparability key hashes the held-fixed block. lasagna results validate recomputes both, so a hand-edited metric no longer matches its own bundle, and a held_fixed edited to fake comparability no longer matches its key. It is not a signature: anyone who edits a number can recompute the id, so rows stay self-reported.

Incomparable results cannot be silently ranked together. Leaderboards group by (benchmark, comparability_key). Rows in one table held the same configuration fixed; rows in different tables are never ranked against each other. A single table of everyone's best number, with different embedding models and sample counts behind it, is the usual way these mislead.

Metric drift is caught. metrics_version is inside the key, so redefining ndcg@10 drops old numbers out of comparison instead of quietly mixing them with new ones.

Reproduction is a signal, not a badge. A row is marked verified only when a different submitter publishes a bundle with the same key whose mean lands inside the reported interval. You cannot verify your own row, and a single-run row can never be verified because it reports no spread to land inside.

docs.title: What it is not
docs.text: Self-reported and machine-validated, not independently reproduced. Nobody is claiming to have rerun anyone's experiment. Stating that plainly is what makes the rest of the guarantees worth anything.

docs.title: Shipping it as a package
docs.text:
Copy examples/lasagna-plugin-template/: a real installable package registering one reranker and one benchmark through entry points, with tests. CI installs and runs it, so it cannot rot into a snippet that no longer works.

[project.entry-points."lasagna_components"]
reranker.my_reranker = "my_pkg:MyReranker"

[project.entry-points.lasagna_benchmarks]
my_dataset = "my_pkg:MyBenchmarkAdapter"

lasagna plugins list

Run it. Discovery logs failures and continues, so a broken entry point does not raise: your component is simply never used, and the results quietly come from the built-in default. lasagna plugins list and lasagna doctor both surface the failure with its exception.

docs.title: Pull request checklist
docs.text:
For a component that goes into Lasagna itself rather than a package of your own. The "PR quality" check tests the description and the diff; a reviewer tests the rest.

  • The component is registered, with paper= and claims= when it implements a published method, so every leaderboard prints the paper's number beside yours.
  • lasagna component validate <target> passes.
  • Any weights it downloads are listed in src/lasagna/core/model_licenses.py.
  • A test under tests/ runs it offline, on a fixture small enough to read.
  • A bundle from lasagna results bundle compares it with a built-in control of its stage, at n_runs: 1 for retrieval with fixed models and 3 or more with an LLM in the loop, and lasagna results validate run.json --strict passes.
  • CHANGELOG.md has a line under Unreleased.
  • The pull request template is filled in, including who read every line of the diff.

The full bar, for every kind of change, is in CONTRIBUTING.md. Methods the project would like to have are listed on Wanted.

docs.title: Known friction
docs.text:
Stated rather than hidden, because you will hit these.

  • Not every benchmark has a corpus of its own. BEIR benchmarks run live against their own corpus. SQuAD v2, HotpotQA, MuSiQue and RAGBench also run live, against a corpus pooled from the samples' gold passages: an easier task than the original, stamped pooled_gold (see the guide, section 8). The rest score generation against gold context only.
  • lasagna component validate checks input mutation for rerankers (the documents), embedders (the list of texts) and generators (the list of contexts), and agentic pipelines (the input data and configuration/model references). Agentic validation supplies a local stub model; pipelines that retrieve still need their retrieval dependencies. Plain functions are not supported for this stage: implement BaseAgenticPipeline. The other stages are handed strings or a file path, which cannot be changed in place. A class component that keeps state should still copy what it is handed before changing it.
  • A single-run row is never marked verified on the results hub, because it reports no spread for another submission to land inside, even when the arms are deterministic. Publish two or more runs if you want a row others can verify.

docs.title: Getting help
docs.text:
lasagna doctor first: it answers most questions before they are asked. Then a bug report, or a component contribution if you want yours listed. If a published number does not reproduce, open a result dispute; run lasagna results compare first, since the field-level diff usually settles it.

Agents working in a repo that uses Lasagna can run lasagna skills install to get the lasagna-component and lasagna-support skills, which encode this document as executable steps.

docs.title: Working with Lasagna
docs.text:
A guide for the thing this package exists to do: find out whether a retrieval component actually helps.

Every Python block below is executed by the release gate on each run (e2e/phases/p3_docs.py). If one stops working, the build fails. Blocks that cannot run hermetically (anything needing a model download or a populated store) are marked and say why.

Contents

  1. The question this answers
  2. Install
  3. The stages you can swap
  4. Write a component
  5. Register it, and see it listed
  6. Compare it against a baseline
  7. Swap it into a pipeline
  8. Measure it on a benchmark
  9. Read and publish the result
  10. Where to go next

docs.title: 1. The question this answers
docs.text:
You have an idea for a reranker, or a chunker, or a query rewriter. The literature says the technique gives +4 NDCG. You want to know whether it helps your corpus, and you want a number you would be willing to publish.

Doing that honestly is harder than it sounds, because the usual approach (fork a RAG pipeline, patch your component in, run it) changes more than one thing at once. Different chunking, a different embedding model, a different top-k, and the +4 you measured belongs to something other than your idea.

Lasagna's answer is that the eight stages are isolated behind typed contracts. You swap exactly one and everything else stays fixed, so a difference in the result is attributable to the swap. That property is enforced by a conformance suite, not by convention.

The rest of this guide walks that workflow end to end.

docs.title: 2. Install
docs.text:
pip install lasagna-rag                    # core: ingest, embed, search, serve
python -m nltk.downloader punkt_tab        # once: nltk's sentence tokenizer data

Lasagna never downloads the tokenizer data by itself. Without it, sentences are split with a regular expression, which can move chunk boundaries, and run bundles record that as the sentence_split_without_punkt fallback.

First run downloads models. The default profile pulls an embedding model on the first upload or search and a reranker on the first search that reranks: about 3.2 GB (BGE-M3, 2.3 GB, and the mxbai reranker, 881 MB; 2.3 GB more with the flag-embedding extra, which fetches BGE-M3's whole repository, ONNX export included), and between 2 and 40 minutes to your first search result on release-gate runs, depending on the connection. After that, a warm search on the speed profile takes tens of milliseconds (median 32 ms over 18,442 chunks on Milvus Lite). The default profile takes 7 to 9 s on two CPU threads, because its large reranker scores every query; more cores or a GPU cut that.

To try it faster, start on the speed profile: dense vector search on a 92 MB model, no reranker and no API key.

lasagna configure --profile speed

Configuration lists the five profiles and what each one downloads, and explains which settings win when a profile, the settings file and the environment disagree.

Nothing in sections 3 to 7 needs a model or a network: components are plain Python objects, and you can exercise them directly. Only section 8 needs a corpus.

docs.title: Extras
docs.text:
Extra Adds eval RAGAS metrics, benchmark loaders, statistics, plots ingest EasyOCR for scanned documents docling structure-aware document conversion (the docling processor) markitdown Microsoft MarkItDown: PDF, Office and HTML to Markdown (the markitdown processor) pymupdf4llm PDF to Markdown (the pymupdf4llm processor); AGPL-3.0 vector-backends Pinecone, Qdrant, Weaviate clients opensearch / pgvector those backends flag-embedding BGE-M3 dense+sparse+ColBERT graphrag entity-linked retrieval llamaindex wrapping LlamaIndex components as stages storage-all S3, GCS, Azure document storage local local LLM inference (HF, Ollama) providers LLM providers beyond OpenAI: Anthropic, Google, Mistral, Cohere, NVIDIA ocr Tesseract and PaddleOCR engines (Tesseract also needs the tesseract program) web web search fallback for corrective RAG lifecycle scheduled document expiry and cleanup production Redis, Celery, Prometheus, OpenTelemetry and PostgreSQL: what settings.lasagna_production.toml turns on all everything above except markitdown, pymupdf4llm and llamaindex

A few components need a package or an API key of their own: the flashrank reranker (pip install flashrank), the cohere reranker and embedder (pip install cohere, COHERE_API_KEY), the voyage embedder (pip install voyageai, VOYAGE_API_KEY) and the openai embedder (OPENAI_API_KEY). Each raises naming what is missing.

all is large: pip takes about two minutes to resolve it (measured with pip 26.2), and uv pip install "lasagna-rag[all]" a few seconds.

docs.title: Platform notes
docs.text:
On Linux x86_64, pip installs the CUDA build of torch, about 3.2 GB of downloads. For CPU only, install torch from the PyTorch CPU index first:

pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu
pip install lasagna-rag

On Apple Silicon, model calls on the GPU (MPS) run one at a time, because two at once crash Metal; concurrent sweep arms wait for each other there. To run everything on the CPU instead, set RAG_USE_GPU=false.

Name collision. pip install lasagna installs a different project (lasagna-ai, an LLM-agent framework), which also provides a top-level lasagna import package. Installing both in one environment makes them overwrite each other. This package is lasagna-rag.

import lasagna loads no torch, transformers, sentence-transformers or pymilvus; those arrive only when something needs them, so a remote-backend client stays light.

No usage telemetry. Lasagna collects none. ragas, the library behind the generation metrics, sends its authors a usage event (its version, the LLM provider and model name, and a random id) each time a judge is built. Importing lasagna turns that off by setting RAGAS_DO_NOT_TRACK=true, unless you have already set it. To send ragas those events, set RAGAS_DO_NOT_TRACK=false before importing lasagna. ragas still writes its random id to a file in your user data folder, but with tracking off it sends nothing.

docs.title: 3. The stages you can swap
docs.text:
from lasagna.core.registry import registry

# list_all() maps each stage to the names registered for it.
for stage, names in sorted(registry.list_all().items()):
    print(f"{stage}: {len(names)} registered -> {', '.join(sorted(names)[:3])}")

From the shell, lasagna component list (or lasagna component list reranker) prints the same, with each component's description and paper.

Each stage has a typed abstract base class. Implementing it is the whole contract: there is no plugin manifest and no registration ceremony beyond one decorator.

Stage Base class Swap it to change Chunker BaseChunker how documents are split Embedder BaseEmbedder what vectors are stored Query enhancer BaseQueryEnhancer how the query is rewritten before retrieval Retriever BaseRetriever how candidates are fetched Reranker BaseReranker the ordering of retrieved candidates Document processor BaseDocumentProcessor how files are parsed Agentic pipeline BaseAgenticPipeline the multi-step retrieval loop Generator BaseGenerator how the answer is written from the retrieved passages

docs.title: 4. Write a component
docs.text:
A reranker takes a query and a list of candidates, and returns them reordered. That is the entire interface:

from lasagna.core.base_components import BaseReranker, ScoredDocument


class LengthReranker(BaseReranker):
    """Ranks by word count. Deliberately unlike retrieval-score order.

    A real component would score query-document relevance. This one is
    obviously wrong on purpose, so that when the ordering changes below you
    know the change came from the swap and not from chance.
    """

    def rerank(self, query, documents, top_k=5, **kwargs):
        import copy

        # Copy first. A stage must not mutate what it was handed: the
        # caller may still be holding those objects, and a component that
        # edits them in place makes results depend on execution order.
        out = [copy.deepcopy(d) for d in documents]
        for d in out:
            d.score = float(len(d.content.split()))
        out.sort(key=lambda d: d.score, reverse=True)
        return out[:top_k]


print("defined:", LengthReranker.__name__)

Two things that matter more than they look:

Deep-copy before you touch anything. The pipeline may hand the same objects to more than one component. A stage that mutates its input makes the result depend on the order stages ran in, which is exactly the kind of hidden coupling this design exists to prevent.

Return at most top_k. The caller decides how many results it wants.

A function is enough for most techniques: @lasagna.reranker("name") on f(query, text) -> score wraps it in this interface, and the other stages have decorators of their own. The README shows one, and Contributing components lists every stage's function signature.

docs.title: 5. Register it, and see it listed
docs.text:
Registration is one decorator. The paper and claims arguments are optional but worth filling in: they are carried through to the listing API and recorded by every run, and on a run of the benchmark a claim names, the leaderboards and results view show the claimed number next to the one you reproduced. Claims are keyed by benchmark (with "split" inside if the paper names one). A metric name runs do not record (ndgc@10) is refused when the component registers, and a benchmark no registry has (beir/scifcat) is a warning naming the closest one.

from lasagna.core.base_components import BaseReranker
from lasagna.core.registry import registry


@registry.register(
    "reranker",
    "length_demo",
    paper="Nobody et al. 2026",
    claims={"beir/scifact": {"ndcg@10": 0.42}},
)
class LengthDemoReranker(BaseReranker):
    def rerank(self, query, documents, top_k=5, **kwargs):
        import copy

        out = [copy.deepcopy(d) for d in documents]
        out.sort(key=lambda d: len(d.content.split()), reverse=True)
        return out[:top_k]


entry = next(e for e in registry.list_rerankers() if e["name"] == "length_demo")
print("implements_contract:", entry["implements_contract"])
print("paper:", entry["paper"])
print("claims:", entry["claims"])

implements_contract is the field to look at. It is True when the class satisfies the abstract base class, not merely when it was registered. A component that registers but does not conform is listed with implements_contract: False, which is how you find out before your results depend on it.

docs.title: Already built in LangChain or LlamaIndex?
docs.text:
lasagna.from_langchain and lasagna.from_llamaindex register an object you already have. A document compressor or node postprocessor becomes a reranker, embeddings become an embedder, and a retriever becomes a retriever. The listing describes the entry as wrapped: langchain.<Class>.

import lasagna
from langchain_core.embeddings import DeterministicFakeEmbedding
from lasagna.core.registry import registry

name = lasagna.from_langchain(DeterministicFakeEmbedding(size=64))
print(name)  # langchain.DeterministicFakeEmbedding
entry = next(e for e in registry.list_embedders() if e["name"] == name)
print(entry["description"])  # wrapped: langchain.DeterministicFakeEmbedding

A sweep run from Python names the returned name like any other component. A sweep file run with lasagna benchmark experiment names the object where you defined it instead: with cohere = CohereRerank(top_n=10) in my_rerankers.py, the arm "my_rerankers:cohere" is wrapped the same way.

Three things to know:

  • A wrapped retriever brings its own index. It searches whatever the object was built over, not the corpus Lasagna ingested. For a benchmark, its index must hold that benchmark's corpus with each corpus id in the metadata (doc_id, or the key you pass as id_key=). A document with no id gets a hash of its text as its id, which matches no relevance judgment.
  • The object's own limits apply. A compressor's top_n or a retriever's k caps how many documents come back; set it at least as high as the pipeline's depth, or the arm is scored on shorter lists than the others.
  • LlamaIndex is an extra: pip install "lasagna-rag[llamaindex]". LangChain needs nothing more.

docs.title: 6. Compare it against a baseline
docs.text:
This is the part that makes a number defensible. Run the same input through two components and compare the outputs. Nothing else varies, so any difference is the component.

import copy

from lasagna.core.base_components import BaseReranker, ScoredDocument


class ByLength(BaseReranker):
    def rerank(self, query, documents, top_k=5, **kwargs):
        out = [copy.deepcopy(d) for d in documents]
        out.sort(key=lambda d: len(d.content.split()), reverse=True)
        return out[:top_k]


class Identity(BaseReranker):
    """Returns candidates untouched, in retrieval order.

    The control. Without it you cannot tell "my component reordered things"
    from "the pipeline never called my component at all": the two look
    identical from the outside.
    """

    def rerank(self, query, documents, top_k=5, **kwargs):
        return [copy.deepcopy(d) for d in documents][:top_k]


candidates = [
    ScoredDocument(content="short one", score=0.9, document_id="d1", chunk_id="c1"),
    ScoredDocument(content="a rather longer passage with more words in it", score=0.5,
                   document_id="d2", chunk_id="c2"),
    ScoredDocument(content="middling length text here", score=0.7,
                   document_id="d3", chunk_id="c3"),
]

baseline = [d.document_id for d in Identity().rerank("q", candidates, top_k=3)]
mine = [d.document_id for d in ByLength().rerank("q", candidates, top_k=3)]

print("baseline order:", baseline)
print("mine:          ", mine)
print("changed:       ", baseline != mine)

# The inputs were not mutated: verify, do not assume.
assert [d.score for d in candidates] == [0.9, 0.5, 0.7]
print("inputs intact:  True")

Always run the control. changed: False has two very different causes (your component agreed with retrieval order, or it never ran), and only the control tells them apart.

docs.title: Picking a baseline that means something
docs.text:
Comparing against any baseline is easy; comparing against a fair one is the work. implements_contract tells you which registered components are interchangeable with yours, which is the set worth comparing against:

from lasagna.core.registry import registry

conforming = [e["name"] for e in registry.list_rerankers() if e["implements_contract"]]
print(f"{len(conforming)} interchangeable rerankers available as baselines")

docs.title: 7. Swap it into a pipeline
docs.text:
Outside a test you want the component running in a real pipeline. replace() swaps one stage and leaves the rest alone.

import copy

from lasagna.core.base_components import BaseReranker
from lasagna.core.pipeline import KnowledgePipeline
from lasagna.core.registry import registry


@registry.register("reranker", "guide_swap_demo")
class SwapDemo(BaseReranker):
    def rerank(self, query, documents, top_k=5, **kwargs):
        return [copy.deepcopy(d) for d in documents][:top_k]


pipeline = KnowledgePipeline(reranker="cross_encoder")
print("before:", type(pipeline.get_component("reranker")).__name__)

pipeline.replace("reranker", "guide_swap_demo")
print("after: ", type(pipeline.get_component("reranker")).__name__)

Check get_component() after replacing, as above. It confirms the swap reached execution rather than only updating a name: a pipeline that kept serving a cached instance would leave you measuring the old component while believing you had changed it.

docs.title: 8. Measure it on a benchmark
docs.text: Sections 4 to 7 prove your component behaves. This section is about whether it helps, which needs a corpus and real metrics.

docs.title: Check the setup first
docs.text:
lasagna benchmark run smoke --profile speed

smoke is 24 documents and 12 queries held inside the package: no dataset download and no API key, and on speed the only model is a 92 MB embedder. It runs the real retrieval pipeline end to end, so a green run means the stack is wired up. lasagna benchmark run measures retrieval unless asked for more; add --tracks retrieval,generation once an LLM key and the [eval] extra are set up, to check answer generation too. It is deliberately easy, so the scores mean "this works", never "this is good".

lasagna benchmark list names every benchmark and lasagna benchmark info describes one. To run on your own questions, see Your own data: a JSONL or CSV file, or a BEIR folder, runs with no adapter to write.

docs.title: Then the real thing
docs.text:
from lasagna.knowledge_evaluation_sdk import Experiment, ExperimentConfig
from lasagna.knowledge_evaluation_sdk.experiment import BenchmarkSpec, PipelineSweepSpec

config = ExperimentConfig(
    name="does my reranker help",
    benchmarks=[BenchmarkSpec(name="beir/scifact", n_samples=200)],
    tracks=["retrieval"],  # NDCG, recall and the rest; no LLM, no judge
    pipeline=PipelineSweepSpec(
        base_profile="speed",  # a 92 MB embedder and no API key
        # Sweep across rerankers with everything else fixed. The comparison is
        # only meaningful because the other seven stages do not move.
        rerankers=["cross_encoder", "length_demo"],
    ),
    # `mode` defaults to "auto": live when the benchmark ships a corpus, so
    # retrieval is actually measured. Say mode="generation_only" only when you
    # want answer quality scored against gold context, with no retrieval.
    n_runs=1,  # retrieval with fixed models gives the same lists every run
)
print(config.mode, "->", len(config.benchmarks), "benchmark(s)")

This one is keyless: speed embeds with a 92 MB model and the cross-encoder control is 92 MB. Name base_profile in every sweep: one without it starts each arm from standard (a 3.2 GB download), while lasagna benchmark run starts from speed. --dry-run and the run header print the profile each arm starts from. The same file in YAML runs with lasagna benchmark experiment sweep.yaml, which is what the README and Contributing components show. Run it, and look at the failed tasks before the scores: a task that failed is listed there, not in the table.

import asyncio

results = asyncio.run(Experiment(config).run())
for task in results.failed_tasks:
    print("failed:", task.task_key, task.error)
print(results.to_markdown("ndcg@10"))

A component override is only measured in live mode. generation_only never constructs the pipeline, so passing reranker= there is a hard error rather than a plausible number scored from gold context. auto picks the right mode and logs which it chose and why.

Benchmarks with no corpus can still measure retrieval, against a pooled corpus, which is easier. SQuAD v2, HotpotQA, MuSiQue and RAGBench ship each question's supporting passages inline and no corpus to search. auto assembles one by pooling those passages across every sample in the run, so each query has to find its own among all the others'. This is a real retrieval task, but a gentler one: HotpotQA and MuSiQue drop their distractor paragraphs at conversion, so the pool holds no hard negatives and recall reads higher than it would against a corpus of the same size. Runs are stamped corpus_provenance: pooled_gold, which is part of the comparability key, so a pooled number can never share a leaderboard row with a BEIR one. For the same questions against a real corpus, use beir/hotpotqa.

Natural Questions and TriviaQA carry no context at all and stay generation_only. There is nothing to pool.

docs.title: How many runs
docs.text:
Retrieval with fixed models is deterministic: the same queries return the same ranked lists on every run. Significance tests pair arms query by query, so the spread they need comes from the queries, and n_runs: 1 gives the same answer as three runs, three times faster. A sweep that repeats identical runs says so when it ends.

Repeat runs when an LLM stage is in the loop. An answer generator, an LLM reranker, HyDE or an agentic pipeline samples, and a model that takes no temperature (see Configuration) varies from run to run whatever you ask for. There, n_runs: 3 or more measures that spread, and variance_source: run keeps the queries fixed so the spread is run to run rather than a resampled subset.

docs.title: When corpus documents fail to ingest
docs.text:
A document that cannot be chunked (an error, or more than 120 s) is left out of the corpus, and the log names it. A partial corpus scores lower than the benchmark would, so every task on it fails, naming the count, the first documents and the setting that accepts it:

ingest_failure_tolerance: 0.02   # up to 2% of the corpus may be missing (at most 0.1)

A run that accepts a partial corpus records it in each result as corpus_ingest_gap (how many documents were ingested, how many failed, and a digest of the ingested ids). That is part of the comparability key, so the run never shares a leaderboard group with one on the complete corpus, and the bundle carries a PARTIAL_CORPUS warning. A later run that reuses the same corpus records the same gap.

docs.title: Sweep the other stages
docs.text:
The same sweep file swaps any stage. Two you will often want:

A retriever. Name it in a config_overrides entry. Put dense, the default vector search as a component, in as the control. Then every arm names its first stage, and the comparison is between retrieval methods:

# retrievers.yaml
name: which first stage
benchmarks:
  - name: beir/scifact
    n_samples: 200
tracks: [retrieval]
pipeline:
  base_profile: speed
  config_overrides:
    - {name: dense, retriever: dense}           # the control
    - {name: bm25, retriever: bm25}
    - {name: hybrid_rrf, retriever: hybrid_rrf}
n_runs: 1

This one is keyless: BM25 needs no model, and speed embeds with the 92 MB one.

A generator. List the answer strategies under generators:. Every arm retrieves the same way, so a difference comes from how the answer was written. concise is the harness's own prompt, word for word, so it is the control:

# generators.yaml
name: how the answer is written
benchmarks:
  - name: hotpotqa
    n_samples: 100
tracks: [generation]
pipeline:
  base_profile: speed
  generators: [concise, cited, chain_of_note]
n_runs: 3          # repeat runs when an LLM stage is in the loop

This one needs an LLM API key and the [eval] extra. cited answers carry [n] markers, and the citation metrics score them. From the shell, lasagna benchmark run <name> --generator cited runs one generator.

An ensemble of rerankers. ensemble averages the scores of the cross-encoders an arm names in ensemble_reranker_models (weights in ensemble_reranker_weights, equal when left out). An arm with fewer than two models, or with one that cannot load, fails instead of scoring as one model:

pipeline:
  base_profile: speed
  config_overrides:
    - {name: minilm, reranker: cross_encoder}       # the control
    - name: ensemble
      reranker: ensemble
      ensemble_reranker_models: [cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2, cross-encoder/ms-marco-TinyBERT-L-2-v2]

mmr and combined (the cross-encoder followed by MMR) run MMR whatever enable_mmr says, since naming them is what turns it on.

Chunkers and embedders sweep as components too (chunkers:, embedders:). Each arm's corpus is chunked or embedded by its own component and kept apart from the other arms' corpora; an embedder also gets its own collection. Every chunking or embedding setting (chunk_size, chunk_unit, embedding_model and so on) gets its own corpus in the same way. An agentic loop is named like a retriever ({name: ircot, agentic_pipeline: ircot}), and each hop it makes searches with the arm's components. Document processors do not sweep: benchmark corpora are loaded as text, so check a processor on your own files.

docs.title: The baselines a reviewer asks for
docs.text:
"Does retrieval help at all?" and "would a long context window do as well?" are answered by arms, not by a separate tool:

# baselines.yaml
name: is retrieval worth it
benchmarks:
  - name: hotpotqa
    n_samples: 100
tracks: [generation]
pipeline:
  base_profile: speed
  config_overrides:
    - {name: rag}                                # the pipeline as configured
    - {name: no_retrieval, no_rag: true}         # answers from the question alone
    - {name: long_context, generator: long_context}
n_runs: 3
  • no_rag: true retrieves nothing: the arm's retrieval track is skipped and it answers with the closed_book generator. It is scored on generation only, so a sweep with tracks: [retrieval] refuses it before anything runs.
  • closed_book is that generator on its own, if you name it under generators:.
  • long_context reads all ten retrieved passages, in rank order, where the default reads five, and the judge sees the same ten.

An arm whose generator reads no passages is not scored on faithfulness or the context metrics, which would be meaningless with no context; the report and the leaderboard say so and point at exact match, token F1 and factual correctness instead. The isolation check files a no_rag arm under the retriever stage.

docs.title: Before a long run: --dry-run
docs.text:
lasagna benchmark experiment sweep.yaml --dry-run              # with a 3-sample probe
lasagna benchmark experiment sweep.yaml --dry-run --no-probe   # nothing runs at all

A dry run prints the arms, the tasks, the models the run loads and whether each is already downloaded, and a token estimate. Unless --no-probe is given it runs three samples per benchmark and extrapolates tokens and time to the whole sweep. Every number is labeled an estimate, and nothing is written under the results folder. For the plugin template's sweep it printed:

Arms (2): reranker=cross_encoder, reranker=template_length
Tasks (2): 1 benchmark x 2 arms x 1 run
  smoke  split=test  12 samples
Models:
  embedder           all-MiniLM-L6-v2  cached
  reranker           cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2  cached
  reranker           component template_length
Tokens: no generation track, so no answer is generated or judged; an arm still calls an LLM if its pipeline does (HyDE, an agentic pipeline, an LLM reranker).
Probe of smoke (estimate): arm 'reranker=cross_encoder' on 3 samples took 2.8 s including setup (loading models, ingesting), 0.12 s per query, 0 LLM calls
  Extrapolated to 24 queries (estimate, every arm assumed to spend what this one did): about 3 s of query time plus setup, 0 system tokens and 0 judge tokens

Dollars only if you ask. A run records tokens, which are observed. Add prices: to the sweep file for an estimate in dollars:

prices: builtin          # the dated table in the package (builtin-2026-10)
# or your own rates, in USD per million tokens, which win over the table:
# prices: {gpt-6-luna: {input_per_1m: 0.10, output_per_1m: 0.50}}

Each task whose tokens all have a rate gets cost_usd_estimate, and the run metadata records the table and the rates used. A rate that holds only for shorter prompts gives no estimate for a task whose calls average longer. With no prices:, a run reports tokens only.

docs.title: Re-running a sweep replays LLM calls
docs.text:
Inside lasagna benchmark experiment, a request asked at temperature 0 that an earlier run made with the same seed is answered from ~/.lasagna/cache/llm.sqlite. A second run of the same sweep, after a crash or with one arm added, then spends no tokens on what it already asked. Token counts read as in the cold run; llm_cache_hits and llm_cache_misses on each task and a hit rate in results.json and the bundle say what was replayed.

What is never replayed:

  • Sampled calls. A response at temperature 0.7 is one draw; replaying it would make repeated runs identical and hide the spread n_runs is meant to measure.
  • The RAGAS judge, which asks for temperature 0.01, unless you set llm_cache: {deterministic_only: false}.
  • Models that take no temperature. The cache replays a call only when temperature 0 was actually sent, so a model the request builder sends no temperature (Claude 4.7 and later, some OpenAI reasoning models) is always called.

A provider of your own, set with set_llm_provider, gets the cache too: the chat model its get_chat_model returns is replayed when temperature 0 was asked for and the model's temperature is 0. A returned object that is not a LangChain chat model cannot carry the cache, and results.json then says "applied": false with the reason under llm_cache.

Turn it off with llm_cache: false in the sweep, --no-cache on the command, or LASAGNA_LLM_CACHE=0. llm_cache: {path: ...} puts the file elsewhere. Nothing is cached outside an experiment, so lasagna serve and the MCP server write no prompt to disk.

docs.title: A development set from your own documents
docs.text:
lasagna benchmark synthesize ./docs --n 200 has an LLM write factoid, multi-hop and unanswerable questions from your files, checks each one with a second call, and writes a JSONL file that lasagna benchmark run takes as is. It is for comparing configurations while you build, not for reported results: questions a model wrote favor systems like that model. Your own data explains why and shows the options.

For what the metrics mean and which are trustworthy, see metrics; for the available datasets, see benchmarks.

docs.title: 9. Read and publish the result
docs.text:
Every run writes a results.json and prints its path. Each command below takes it.

Question Command Is the gap real, across every pair of arms? lasagna results significance results.json --all Could this run have detected the effect I care about? lasagna results power results.json baseline candidate Do two techniques compose, or overlap? lasagna results interaction results.json (a 2x2 run) Which queries did an arm lose, at retrieval or generation? lasagna results per-query results.json --sort-by ndcg@10 Are two runs comparable at all? lasagna results compare a.json b.json

significance runs a paired sign-flip test on every pair of arms and corrects the p-values with Holm-Bonferroni, then ends in a box that says what the table supports: green names each pair that survives and which side won; yellow says nothing survived and points at power.

Hand someone the whole run as one page:

lasagna results view results.json -o view.html

The page carries the versions and run id, the stage isolation check, and per benchmark the leaderboard, the significance table with its verdict, every metric per arm, and a per-query diff between two arms (--diff A B, default the top two) with what each one retrieved. It is one file with no external requests, so it opens offline and can be attached to a review.

Put a leaderboard in a paper:

mkdir -p bundles
lasagna results bundle results.json -o bundles/run.json
lasagna results leaderboard bundles/ --format latex

--format latex prints one booktabs table per comparability group (rows in one table held the same configuration fixed; rows in different tables are never ranked together), or writes one .tex file per benchmark with -o. Arm names are escaped for LaTeX.

Every results command that reads a bundle checks it as results validate does. A bundle that fails (a number edited after it was made, missing provenance) is refused with its problems listed, or left out of a folder's leaderboard with its name printed. --allow-invalid on leaderboard and view shows it anyway, every number marked INVALID. A results.json is not a bundle, and is shown as not validated.

Publish a number someone else can check:

lasagna results bundle results.json -o run.json
lasagna results validate run.json

The bundle carries the library versions, hardware, resolved sweep, corpus fingerprint and comparability key, and validate recomputes the key, the run id and every aggregate from the per-query scores. It also lists integrity warnings that do not invalidate a bundle, such as SINGLE_RUN (one run of a pipeline in which something samples) or UNRESOLVED_JUDGE_ALIAS (a judge named by a floating alias); --strict turns them into failures. A run records nothing_samples when only retrieval ran and no task called an LLM; one run of it is complete and raises no SINGLE_RUN. The results hub runs a public leaderboard from such bundles, and marks a row verified only when someone else's bundle reproduces it: within its spread, which needs at least two runs, or by equalling its mean when nothing in the run samples.

docs.title: Two warnings
docs.text:
Check the model license before publishing. Several strong rerankers are non-commercial. lasagna.core.model_licenses warns once at load, and model-licenses lists the terms per model.

A component that conforms is not a component that helps. Everything up to section 7 proves your code is wired in correctly. Only section 8 tells you whether it improves retrieval, and only a significance test over enough queries tells a real gap from noise.

docs.title: Model licenses
docs.text:
Lasagna ships no model weights. Every embedding, reranking and sparse-encoding model is downloaded from its upstream host (usually the Hugging Face Hub) the first time you use it, and each carries its own license, independent of Lasagna's Apache 2.0.

Most are permissive. Four are not, and they are selectable on purpose: Lasagna exists to compare RAG components, and excluding well-known models would undercut that. What matters is that you know which one you picked.

Short version: for research, evaluation and benchmarking, everything below is fine. Before putting a configuration into a commercial product, check this page: four models forbid that use, or do not say they allow it.

Sparse retrieval is opt-in, so this loads only when you enable it. jinaai/jina-reranker-v2-base-multilingual CC-BY-NC-4.0 Reranker option Non-commercial. docs.title: Checking programmatically
docs.text:
from lasagna.core.model_licenses import describe, is_commercial_use_restricted, restricted_models

# LicenseInfo(spdx='CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0', commercial_use=False, url='https://huggingface.co/...', note=...)

from lasagna.core.config import get_rag_config

docs.title: Bringing your own model
docs.text:
Lasagna does not restrict which model identifier you configure. Models absent from the table load normally and log a DEBUG note that their license was not checked. Absence means uncataloged, not unrestricted.

If you add a model to the configurator, add it to src/lasagna/core/model_licenses.py too. tests/test_model_licenses.py fails the build when the UI offers a model the table does not cover, which is what keeps this page honest.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
This table is a convenience, not legal advice, and licenses change. The model card linked from each entry is authoritative; confirm there before relying on anything here.

Lasagna also redistributes no benchmark corpora; evaluation datasets are fetched from their official sources and carry their own terms.

docs.title: Your own data
docs.text:
Run a sweep on your own questions with no adapter to write: a JSONL or CSV file, or a folder in the BEIR layout. You can also have an LLM write a development set from your documents (see Synthetic questions).

lasagna benchmark validate-data my_data.jsonl              # check it, see what it supports
lasagna benchmark run my_data.jsonl --profile speed            # retrieval, keyless

In a sweep, name the file with path: instead of name:. A relative path is read from the sweep file's folder:

benchmarks:
  - {path: data/my_data.jsonl, n_samples: 50}
  - {path: data/support_tickets.csv, name: tickets}   # optional display name
  - {path: data/my_beir}                              # a BEIR folder

docs.title: JSONL
docs.text:
One JSON object per line. Only question is required.

Field Type Meaning question string The question. answer or answers string, or list of strings The reference answer. With a list, exact match and token F1 accept any of them; the first is the reference the judge sees. contexts or context list of strings, or one string The passages that answer the question. id string or number The question's id. Defaults to row<line number>. Must be unique. expected_docs list of strings Names for the passages in contexts, in the same order: contexts[i] is the text of expected_docs[i]. Use it when several rows cite the same document by name. metadata object Anything else. metadata.unanswerable: true marks a question with no answer; a row with it has no answer (or "answer": ""). Other keys can be used as filters: on the benchmark entry. 
{"id": "q1", "question": "What does the soda add to soda-lime glass?", "answer": "It lowers the melting point of the silica.", "contexts": ["Soda-lime glass is made by melting silica sand with sodium carbonate and calcium oxide. The soda lowers the melting point of the silica from about 1700 to roughly 1000 degrees Celsius."]}
{"id": "q2", "question": "Who introduced the solidus?", "answers": ["Constantine the Great", "Constantine I"], "context": "The solidus was a gold coin introduced by Constantine the Great in roughly 312 AD."}
{"id": "q3", "question": "What did the solidus cost to mint?", "contexts": ["The solidus was a gold coin introduced by Constantine the Great in roughly 312 AD."], "metadata": {"unanswerable": true}}

Any other field is an error that names the field, so a typo such as anwser is caught instead of silently leaving every row without an answer. Put fields of your own under metadata.

docs.title: CSV
docs.text:
A header row is required. The columns are question (required), answer, contexts and id. Separate several passages in one contexts cell with |||. CSV cannot mark a question unanswerable; use JSONL for that.

id,question,answer,contexts
q1,Who introduced the solidus?,Constantine the Great,The solidus was a gold coin introduced by Constantine the Great in roughly 312 AD.
q2,What replaced the debased solidus?,The hyperpyron,The hyperpyron replaced the debased solidus after the monetary reform of Alexios I Komnenos in 1092.|||Debasement of the solidus began in earnest under Nikephoros II.

docs.title: BEIR folder
docs.text:
The layout of BEIR's own downloads:

my_beir/
  corpus.jsonl      {"_id": "d1", "title": "...", "text": "..."}
  queries.jsonl     {"_id": "q1", "text": "..."}
  qrels/test.tsv    query-id <tab> corpus-id <tab> score   (header optional)

Each qrels/<split>.tsv is a split, chosen with split:. A score above 0 marks a document relevant; graded scores feed NDCG. A judgment that names a document or query missing from the folder is an error, with the count and the first few ids.

docs.title: What each format can measure
docs.text:
Data Retrieval Generation BEIR folder yes, against its corpus no (no answers) JSONL or CSV with contexts and answers yes, against every row's contexts pooled into one corpus yes JSONL or CSV with answers and no contexts no (nothing to retrieve) closed-book only, with the closed_book generator

Retrieval on a file with contexts searches a pool of every row's passages: each question has to find its own among all the others. That pool holds only gold passages, with no hard negatives, so it is an easier search than a real corpus of the same size. Results are labeled corpus_provenance: pooled_gold and never share a leaderboard group with results on a real corpus. A passage that several rows share is one document, relevant to each of them. The passages of an unanswerable row join the pool but are relevant to nothing.

A run that asks for a track the data cannot support is refused before any model loads, with the reason and the fix.

docs.title: Names, checkpoints and comparisons
docs.text:
A file registers as local/<stem>@<12 hex digits> (data/my_data.jsonl as local/my_data@ and the digits; a BEIR folder as local/<folder name>@...), the start of the sha256 of its bytes (for a BEIR folder, of the files read from it), or as <name>@<12 hex digits> when the entry gives name:. The full digest is recorded as the dataset revision. Because the hash is in the benchmark name:

  • an edited file is a different benchmark, so --resume never restores a result computed on the old version and the old corpus is never reused;
  • two files with different content never share a leaderboard group or a comparability key, even under the same file name;
  • the same bytes under the same name are the same benchmark, on any machine.

lasagna benchmark validate-data prints the name a file will run under.

docs.title: Synthetic questions from your documents
docs.text:
lasagna benchmark synthesize ./docs --n 200 --out my_bench.jsonl \
    --mix factoid=0.6,multihop=0.3,unanswerable=0.1 --seed 42 --dry-run

This reads every supported file under ./docs (.md and .txt as plain text, PDF, DOCX and HTML through the same extractor as an upload), cuts each into 200-word passages with the fixed chunker, and asks an LLM for three kinds of question:

  • factoid: answered by a short fact in one passage;
  • multihop: needs a fact from each of two passages in two different documents (the second passage is the one sharing the most words with the first);
  • unanswerable: on the subject of a passage, but not answered by it.

A second call checks each question. An answer must be supported by its source passages; an unanswerable question must not be answered by its passage or by the three passages sharing the most words with it. Rows that fail are dropped and counted, so the file can hold fewer than --n rows; the summary says how many and why.

--dry-run prints the plan (documents, passages, questions of each type, LLM calls) and a token estimate, calls no LLM and writes nothing. Without --dry-run an LLM is needed: set an API key variable such as OPENAI_API_KEY or ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (without one, the error lists every variable read), and MODEL_NAME or --model to choose the model. Calls ask for temperature 0 (a model that takes no temperature is sent none; see Configuration). The same folder, seed and model give the same plan and the same prompts.

The output is the JSONL format above. Each row records how it was made:

{"id": "synth-0001", "question": "...", "answer": "...", "contexts": ["..."],
 "metadata": {"question_type": "factoid", "source_doc_ids": ["guide.md"],
              "prompt_id": "factoid-v1", "prompt_sha256": "...", "model": "...",
              "seed": 42, "synthetic": true, "unanswerable": false}}

filters: {question_type: multihop} on the benchmark entry scores one type.

From Python:

from lasagna.knowledge_evaluation_sdk.synthesize import synthesize, write_jsonl

rows = synthesize("docs", n=200, mix="factoid=0.6,multihop=0.3,unanswerable=0.1", seed=42)
write_jsonl(rows, "my_bench.jsonl")

docs.title: Synthetic sets are for development, not for claims
docs.text:
A question an LLM wrote from a passage tends to reuse that passage's words and the model's own phrasing. A retriever finds such questions easier than the ones your users ask, and a pipeline built on the same family of models finds them easier still, so scores on a synthetic set read high, and favor the systems most like the model that wrote it. The answerability check is made by that same model and inherits its mistakes.

Use a synthetic set to compare configurations on your own documents while you build. Report results on human-written questions: a public benchmark, or a set your users or annotators wrote.

A RAG pipeline in Lasagna is eight stages behind typed contracts. A component fills one stage, and the stages around it cannot tell which one is there. That is what lets a sweep change one stage and hold the rest fixed.
