docs.title: Comparability and provenance
docs.text: Two numbers can be compared only if everything except the thing under test was held fixed. Nothing in a plain results table says what was held fixed. Lasagna records it, and hashes it into a comparability key.

docs.title: The comparability key
docs.text:
The key is a 16-character hash over the configuration a comparison holds fixed:

  • the metrics version
  • the benchmark, split, number of samples, sampling seed and sample-id digest
  • the corpus fingerprint and its provenance
  • the resolved run mode
  • the embedder model and dimension
  • the chunker
  • the retriever's top-k
  • the vector backend
  • the judge model
  • BM25 stemming
  • the stage-manifest digest of every stage the run does not vary

The key excludes the dimension under test. That is the design. If the key covered everything, no two rows would be comparable. If it covered nothing, all rows would be comparable no matter what they measured. The dimension under test is recorded separately as varied_dimensions.

A field that was not captured is recorded as missing, so it hashes differently from a field that was captured. An unknown embedder cannot match a known one.

docs.title: The metrics version
docs.text: The metrics version is part of the key. If the definition of NDCG@10 changes, old numbers fall out of comparison instead of being mixed with new ones. This release is metrics version 1.7. Results from earlier builds never share a leaderboard group with it.

docs.title: Provenance in a bundle
docs.text:
lasagna results bundle packages a run with what a reader needs to judge it:

  • the Lasagna version, Python version and platform, with no paths or host names
  • the resolved sweep
  • the corpus fingerprint
  • the comparability key of each benchmark and arm
  • the per-query scores
  • the integrity warnings and blocking problems

lasagna results validate recomputes the key, the run id and every aggregate from the per-query scores. A number edited after the run no longer matches.

That is an integrity check against mistakes and simple edits. It is not a signature: anyone who edits a number can recompute the run id. The hub therefore treats results as self-reported.

docs.title: Leaderboards group by key
docs.text: A leaderboard groups rows by benchmark and comparability key. Rows in one group held the same configuration fixed, so you can rank them. Rows in different groups are never ranked together. Use lasagna results compare a.json b.json to see the field-level difference between two runs.

docs.title: Reproduction by collision
docs.text: The results hub marks a row verified when a different submitter's bundle with the same comparability key lands inside the row's mean and spread. When nothing in the run samples, the hub accepts an exact match of the mean.

docs.title: Significance testing
docs.text: lasagna results significance answers one question: is the gap between two arms larger than the noise in your queries? This page says how it decides, and why it uses these methods.

docs.title: The paired sign-flip test
docs.text:
For each query, take the score of arm A minus the score of arm B. These are the paired differences. If the arms were equivalent, each difference would be as likely to be positive as negative. So every way of flipping the signs is equally likely.

The p-value is the share of sign patterns whose summed difference is at least as large, in absolute value, as the one you observed.

  • A difference of exactly zero cannot change sign. It drops out.
  • With at most 30 non-zero differences, Lasagna lists every pattern, so the p-value is exact.
  • Above that, it draws random patterns (10,000 by default) and reports (count + 1) / (draws + 1), which is never exactly zero.
  • Scores are averaged across runs of the same arm first, so repeated runs do not count as extra queries.

Alongside the p-value you get a 95% confidence interval for the mean difference, from a t distribution, and Cohen's d_z for the paired design (mean / std of the differences).

docs.title: Why not a bootstrap
docs.text: RAG evaluations often have 10 to 50 queries. At that size the sign-flip test with a t interval holds its stated level. The paired bootstrap that Lasagna used before did not: at 12 to 20 queries it rejected a true null 8 to 9 percent of the time at alpha 0.05.

docs.title: Many arms: Holm-Bonferroni
docs.text:
Compare ten arms and you have 45 pairs. At alpha 0.05, a few pairs will look significant by chance. significance corrects for that with the Holm-Bonferroni step-down procedure:

  1. Sort the p-values from smallest to largest.
  2. Compare the smallest with alpha / m, the next with alpha / (m - 1), and so on.
  3. Stop at the first p-value that fails. It and every larger one are not significant.

This controls the chance of any false positive across the whole family, and it is less strict than a plain Bonferroni correction.

docs.title: Reading the verdict box
docs.text:
The table ends in a box.

  • Green names each pair that survives the correction and says which side won.
  • Yellow says no pair survived and points at lasagna results power.

Yellow does not mean the arms are the same. Either they are the same, or the run was too small to tell. power separates the two.

docs.title: Power
docs.text:
lasagna results power results.json baseline candidate reports the smallest difference the run could have detected. Given the spread of the paired differences, it computes the minimum detectable effect for the significance level and power you ask for (alpha 0.05 and power 0.80 by default).

It is computed after the run, from the variance the run actually showed. An up-front calculation would need a variance estimate that nobody has before the run. If your observed difference is smaller than the minimum detectable effect, the honest conclusion is "inconclusive", not "no difference". The report also carries the pair's own uncorrected p-value, because a difference below the minimum can still be significant.

docs.title: Interaction
docs.text:
lasagna results interaction takes a 2x2 run and asks whether two techniques compose. It estimates the double difference:

interaction = (both - neither) - ((only A - neither) + (only B - neither))

Positive means the techniques compound. Negative means they overlap, because both fix the same errors. Two papers cannot answer this, because the interaction is not a function of the two separate gains. See the paper study for why it matters.

docs.title: Where the code lives
docs.text: The methods are BenchmarkResults.significance_test, pairwise_significance, minimum_detectable_effect and interaction_test in results.py. The metrics reference gives every parameter and return key.

docs.title: Stage isolation
docs.text: A comparison tells you something only when the two arms differ in the one thing you changed. Lasagna splits a pipeline into eight stages and checks, at run time, that a swap stayed inside its stage.

docs.title: The eight stages
docs.text:
document_processor -> chunker -> embedder -> retriever -> query_enhancer
                                             -> reranker -> agentic_pipeline -> generator

Each stage has a fixed interface. A reranker takes a query and candidates and returns them ranked. A chunker takes text and returns chunks. Because the interface is fixed, you can swap one component for another and leave the other seven stages alone. The catalog lists the stages and their contracts, and the write a component guide shows how to fill one.

docs.title: What the check does
docs.text:
Each task records a stage manifest. The manifest is a digest of every setting and every component that reached each stage. After the sweep, Lasagna compares the manifests of all arms against what each arm said it would change.

Two things count as a failure:

  • Undeclared change. A stage differs between two arms, but neither arm named it. A setting leaked across a stage boundary, for example through a profile default.
  • Inert change. An arm names a change that its manifest does not show. The setting or component never reached the pipeline, so the arm's number is the baseline's under another name.

The run prints both. lasagna results validate refuses a bundle with an undeclared change, and lasagna results view shows the check on its page.

docs.title: What the check does not see
docs.text:
The manifest digests configuration, not behavior. A component that changes state outside its stage while it runs, such as patching another module, leaves every digest unchanged and passes the check. Two other guards cover that case:

  • The stage contracts, which say what a component may touch.
  • The conformance tests. lasagna component validate <module:Class> runs them against your component. See Contributing components.

docs.title: Strict stages
docs.text: A stage that cannot run fails the task. If you ask for query expansion and no LLM is configured, or an agentic search errors, the task fails. It does not fall back to the baseline and report the baseline's score under the arm's name.

docs.title: Settings that do not count
docs.text: Some settings change how a run is operated, not what it computes. A cache backend, a connection pool size and a log level are examples. They stay out of the manifest, so they never read as a change to the system under test.

docs.title: How the paper used Lasagna
docs.text: Lasagna is the framework behind the paper Retrieval Augmented Generation Compositionality by Ido Levy, Segev Shlomov and Leshem Choshen (2026). This page says what the study asked and how the framework made it possible. For the full results, read the paper.

docs.title: The question
docs.text:
RAG papers report one component at a time. A new reranker is measured against a baseline with no query expansion and an old chunker. If a reranker claims +4 NDCG and a query expander claims +3, you cannot tell from the papers whether stacking them gives +7, +4 or -1.

The study asks whether gains measured one component at a time survive when the components are combined.

docs.title: The design
docs.text:
The study tests 450 configurations across eight benchmarks, with corpora from 5K to 200K documents. Eight design dimensions vary across the configurations.

To attribute a difference to a single change, every other part of the pipeline has to stay fixed. That needs a pipeline with swappable stages and a harness that checks the swap. Lasagna provides both: the stages, the comparability key and the significance tests.

docs.title: What it found
docs.text:
Finding Predicted Realized Retrieval gains do not add up: the three strongest single techniques, combined (NDCG@10) +47% +17% Faithfulness gains do carry over: one factor at a time versus the best full pipeline +28% +32%

The best pipeline also changes with corpus size. At 200K documents, the design that leads at small corpora trails by 13.7% NDCG@10, and the rank flip is visible from 25K.

docs.title: What the paper calls the profiles
docs.text: The paper's Max-Reliable profile is max_quality in the code. See profiles and configuration.

docs.title: Run your own version
docs.text:
You can ask the same question about your own components. Run the arms alone and together, then use lasagna results interaction on the 2x2. The compare a component guide shows how to write the sweep.

Lasagna does not ship the paper's per-query results or a prebuilt index. The pre-registration has the study's plan.

docs.title: Your first comparison
docs.text: You will write a reranker in six lines, check it, and test it against a cross-encoder inside a full pipeline. The first part needs no model and no corpus. The sweep needs no API key.

docs.title: 1. Write the technique
docs.text:
Put this in my_ideas.py. The decorator wraps your function in the reranker interface and registers it. paper and claims are optional. They are recorded with every run that uses the component.

# my_ideas.py
import lasagna

@lasagna.reranker(paper="Doe et al. 2026", claims={"beir/scifact": {"ndcg@10": 0.456}})
def keyword_overlap(query, text):  # your technique: score one passage
    return len(set(query.lower().split()) & set(text.lower().split()))

if __name__ == "__main__":  # try it on three passages
    from lasagna.core.base_components import ScoredDocument
    from lasagna.core.registry import registry

    candidates = [
        ScoredDocument(content="short", score=0.9, document_id="d1", chunk_id="c1"),
        ScoredDocument(content="a considerably longer passage of text", score=0.5,
                       document_id="d2", chunk_id="c2"),
        ScoredDocument(content="middling length here", score=0.7,
                       document_id="d3", chunk_id="c3"),
    ]

    mine = registry.get("reranker", "keyword_overlap").rerank("length of a passage", candidates)
    entry = next(e for e in registry.list_rerankers() if e["name"] == "keyword_overlap")
    print("retrieval order:", [d.document_id for d in candidates])
    print("my reranker:    ", [d.document_id for d in mine])
    print("claims recorded:", entry["claims"])
    print("interchangeable:", entry["implements_contract"])

python my_ideas.py

retrieval order: ['d1', 'd2', 'd3']
my reranker:     ['d2', 'd3', 'd1']
claims recorded: {'beir/scifact': {'ndcg@10': 0.456}}
interchangeable: True

interchangeable: True means the component satisfies its stage's interface, so a comparison against a built-in measures your idea and not an interface difference.

docs.title: 2. Test it inside a full pipeline
docs.text:
Save this as sweep.yaml. One arm is a built-in cross-encoder, the control. The other is yours. Every other stage stays fixed.

name: does keyword_overlap help
benchmarks: [{name: smoke}]
tracks: [retrieval]
pipeline:
  base_profile: speed
  rerankers: [cross_encoder, "my_ideas:keyword_overlap"]
n_runs: 1

lasagna benchmark experiment sweep.yaml

The first run downloads 183 MB once (a 92 MB embedder and a 92 MB cross-encoder). Look at the failed tasks before the scores. A task that failed is listed there and not in the table.

docs.title: 3. Ask whether the difference is real
docs.text:
lasagna results significance "<output>/results.json" -m ndcg@10 --all

Replace <output> with the folder the run printed. The command tests every pair of arms with a paired sign-flip test, corrects the p-values with Holm, and ends with a box that says what the table supports. For a real run on 100 SciFact queries, see step 4 of Contributing a component. To switch from the 12-query smoke benchmark to a real one, name beir/scifact and set n_samples.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Lasagna runs on Python 3.10 to 3.13.

pip install lasagna-rag                    # core: ingest, embed, search, serve
python -m nltk.downloader punkt_tab        # once: nltk's sentence tokenizer data

Lasagna never downloads the tokenizer data by itself. Without it, sentences are split with a regular expression, which can move chunk boundaries. Run bundles record that as the sentence_split_without_punkt fallback.

The package is lasagna-rag

pip install lasagna installs a different project (lasagna-ai, an LLM-agent framework). It also provides a top-level lasagna import package, so installing both in one environment makes them overwrite each other.

docs.title: What the first run downloads
docs.text:
The default profile pulls an embedding model on the first upload or search and a reranker on the first search that reranks. That is about 3.2 GB: BGE-M3 (2.3 GB) and the mxbai reranker (881 MB). The flag-embedding extra adds 2.3 GB more, because it fetches BGE-M3's whole repository, ONNX export included. Expect between 2 and 40 minutes to your first search result on release-gate runs. The spread is your connection.

To try Lasagna faster, start on the speed profile: dense vector search on a 92 MB model, no reranker and no API key.

lasagna configure --profile speed

Configuration lists the five profiles and what each one downloads.

docs.title: Pin the versions the release was tested with
docs.text:
For a result you want to repeat later, install with the constraints file from the release. It was resolved on Python 3.12 and needs 3.12 or later, because numpy does not install on 3.10 or 3.11 with those pins.

pip install "lasagna-rag[eval]==0.1.0" -c https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dolev31/lasagna/v0.1.0/constraints/0.1.0.txt

A few components need a package or an API key of their own: the flashrank reranker (pip install flashrank), the cohere reranker and embedder (pip install cohere, COHERE_API_KEY), the voyage embedder (pip install voyageai, VOYAGE_API_KEY) and the openai embedder (OPENAI_API_KEY). Each raises an error that names what is missing.

all is large. pip takes about two minutes to resolve it (measured with pip 26.2), and uv pip install "lasagna-rag[all]" a few seconds.

docs.title: An LLM for the generation track
docs.text:
Retrieval comparisons need no LLM. The generation track, the judged metrics and LLM-based components (HyDE, an LLM reranker, an agentic pipeline) do.

With no LLM configured, Lasagna uses the first API key it finds in the environment, in the order of the provider table, with that provider's default model. Set MODEL_NAME to pick another model on that provider.

  • The core install talks to OpenAI, Azure OpenAI and OpenAI-compatible endpoints.
  • Anthropic, Google, Mistral, Cohere and NVIDIA need the providers extra.
  • A local Hugging Face model needs the local extra.
  • Groq, watsonx and llama.cpp need their LangChain package.

In an experiment, the answers come from RAG_EVAL_GENERATOR_MODEL, else MODEL_NAME, else the provider default. The judge is separate: RAG_EVAL_JUDGE_MODEL, else judge_model: in the sweep file, else gpt-6-luna. To write your own provider, see the providers package.

docs.title: Platform notes
docs.text:
On Linux x86_64, pip installs the CUDA build of torch, about 3.2 GB of downloads. For CPU only, install torch from the PyTorch CPU index first:

pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu
pip install lasagna-rag

On Apple Silicon, model calls on the GPU (MPS) run one at a time, because two at once crash Metal. Concurrent sweep arms wait for each other there. To run everything on the CPU instead, set RAG_USE_GPU=false. The install weighs about 1.3 GB on macOS arm64.

import lasagna loads no torch, transformers, sentence-transformers or pymilvus. Those arrive only when something needs them, so a remote-backend client stays light.

docs.title: Telemetry
docs.text: Lasagna collects no usage data. ragas, the library behind the generation metrics, sends its authors a usage event (its version, the LLM provider and model name, and a random id) each time a judge is built. Importing lasagna turns that off by setting RAGAS_DO_NOT_TRACK=true, unless you have already set it. To send ragas those events, set RAGAS_DO_NOT_TRACK=false before importing lasagna. ragas still writes its random id to a file in your user data folder, but with tracking off it sends nothing.

docs.title: The offline acceptance demo
docs.text:
examples/acceptance/offline_demo.py runs every feature of Lasagna 0.1.0 end to end, offline, in under five minutes. It is in the source checkout, not in the wheel.

git clone https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna.git
cd lasagna
pip install -e ".[eval]"
python examples/acceptance/offline_demo.py

It has eight steps, and each one does what a user would do and checks what the user would see:

  1. benchmark synthesize --dry-run calls no LLM and writes nothing. The real run writes 12 questions from the smoke documents, each marked synthetic.
  2. benchmark validate-data accepts that file and names the row and the field of a deliberately broken copy.
  3. lasagna.from_langchain turns a LangChain-style document compressor into a reranker.
  4. benchmark experiment --dry-run lists the arms, tasks and models of the sweep and writes no results.
  5. The sweep runs five arms (dense, the wrapped reranker, closed_book, long_context and no_rag: true) on both tracks.
  6. The same sweep again replays every LLM response from the cache: hit rate 1.0, no LLM call, the same numbers.
  7. results bundle, results view and results leaderboard --format latex.
  8. lasagna-mcp --help answers in under 2 s, and the server's default tool list has no tool that deletes data.

Nothing needs a network or an API key. A deterministic stub stands in for the LLM, put in through set_llm_provider, so token counting, temperature pinning and the response cache run as they do for a real provider. Retrieval is real: it uses the speed profile's all-MiniLM-L6-v2 from the Hugging Face cache with HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1, and a socket guard refuses every connection that is not to your machine. The demo makes its own home folder inside its working folder, so your ~/.lasagna is left alone.

It prints one line per step with its time. It exits 1 at the first failed check, with the reason. Exit 2 means it could not start, for example because a model is not in the cache. Run it once with --download-models to fetch the model, and use --workdir DIR to choose where it works.

docs.title: The notebook
docs.text: Compare your reranker opens in Google Colab. It tests a reranker on 100 SciFact queries over the full corpus, with a cross-encoder as the control. It prints the significance table, runs the stage isolation check and writes a validated bundle. It needs no API key and is stored without outputs. The same code is in examples/notebooks/compare_your_reranker.py.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: This page indexes one document and searches it, on the speed profile: a 92 MB model, no reranker, no LLM and no API key.

docs.title: From Python
docs.text:
import asyncio
from lasagna.sdk import KnowledgeClient, config_for_speed

async def main():
    client = KnowledgeClient(session_id="quickstart", config=config_for_speed())
    doc = await client.upload("paper.pdf")
    await client.documents.wait_for_processing(doc.document_id)  # upload returns once queued
    results = await client.search_documents("What did the ablation show?")
    for r in results.results:
        print(f"[{r.score:.2f}] {r.chunk.content[:120]}")
    await client.close()

asyncio.run(main())

upload() returns once the file is queued, so wait for processing before you search. wait_for_processing raises DocumentProcessingError with the reason and the fix if the file cannot be indexed.

Run it twice and the second run uploads nothing new: the document is reported with duplicate_of. Pass allow_duplicates=True to index it again.

docs.title: From the shell
docs.text:
lasagna configure --profile speed
lasagna upload paper.pdf
lasagna search "what did the ablation show?"

lasagna init asks the same questions interactively. lasagna upload --force indexes a file again.

To serve the same index over HTTP, run:

lasagna serve

That starts the REST API and the configuration page on 127.0.0.1:8000. While it runs, the CLI asks the server instead of opening the store itself, because a local store opens in one process at a time.

docs.title: What to expect
docs.text:
These timings are from an M1 Max (10 cores, 64 GB) on the speed profile:

Step Time First run, including the 92 MB model download 30 to 35 s First run, model already cached 8 s One search, one document (median of ten) 15 ms One search over 18,442 chunks on Milvus Lite (median) 32 ms One lasagna search command about 10 s

A CLI command is slow because each one loads the model and opens the store. Use lasagna serve or the Python client when you search more than once.

The default profile (BGE-M3 plus the mxbai reranker) downloads about 3.2 GB and takes 117 ms per warm search on the M1 Max GPU and 3.1 s on two CPU threads.

docs.title: How settings are kept
docs.text: Settings belong to a session. Each session has its own embedding model, and its data lives in ~/.lasagna. A client created without config= reads the session's saved settings. See Configuration for the rules about which setting wins.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Your first comparison tests a reranker of your own.

docs.title: Baselines
docs.text:
"Does retrieval help at all?" and "would a long context window do as well?" are answered by arms in a sweep, not by a separate tool.

name: is retrieval worth it
benchmarks:
  - name: hotpotqa
    n_samples: 100
tracks: [generation]
pipeline:
  base_profile: speed
  config_overrides:
    - {name: rag}                                # the pipeline as configured
    - {name: no_retrieval, no_rag: true}         # answers from the question alone
    - {name: long_context, generator: long_context}
n_runs: 3

This sweep needs an LLM API key and the eval extra.

docs.title: The three arms
docs.text:
• rag is the pipeline as configured.
  • no_rag: true retrieves nothing. The arm's retrieval track is skipped and it answers with the closed_book generator, which sees the question alone. The arm is scored on generation only, so a sweep with tracks: [retrieval] refuses it before anything runs.
  • long_context reads all ten retrieved passages in rank order, where the default reads five, and the judge sees the same ten.

closed_book is also a generator on its own. Name it under generators: if you want it as an arm without the no_rag flag.

docs.title: Arms with no passages
docs.text:
An arm whose generator reads no passages is not scored on faithfulness or the context metrics, because those would be meaningless with no context. The report and the leaderboard say so and point at exact match, token F1 and factual correctness instead.

The stage isolation check files a no_rag arm under the retriever stage, so a run that varies only that flag passes the check.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Compare a component covers the rest of the sweep file.

docs.title: Compare a component
docs.text: A sweep file names the arms, and Lasagna runs each arm through the same pipeline with everything else held fixed. This page covers the sweep file, the stages you can sweep, and how to read the verdict.

docs.title: Check the setup first
docs.text:
lasagna benchmark run smoke --profile speed

smoke is 24 documents and 12 queries held inside the package. There is no dataset download and no API key, and on speed the only model is a 92 MB embedder. A green run means the stack is wired up. The command measures retrieval unless asked for more. Add --tracks retrieval,generation once an LLM key and the eval extra are set up. The scores mean "this works", never "this is good".

lasagna benchmark list names every benchmark and lasagna benchmark info describes one. The benchmark catalog lists them all.

docs.title: Write the sweep
docs.text:
name: does my reranker help
benchmarks:
  - name: beir/scifact
    n_samples: 200
tracks: [retrieval]            # NDCG, recall and the rest; no LLM, no judge
pipeline:
  base_profile: speed          # a 92 MB embedder and no API key
  rerankers: [cross_encoder, "my_ideas:keyword_overlap"]
n_runs: 1

lasagna benchmark experiment sweep.yaml

Name base_profile in every sweep. Without it, each arm starts from standard (a 3.2 GB download), while lasagna benchmark run starts from speed. The run header and --dry-run print the profile each arm starts from.

The same sweep in Python:

import asyncio
from lasagna.knowledge_evaluation_sdk import Experiment, ExperimentConfig
from lasagna.knowledge_evaluation_sdk.experiment import BenchmarkSpec, PipelineSweepSpec

config = ExperimentConfig(
    name="does my reranker help",
    benchmarks=[BenchmarkSpec(name="beir/scifact", n_samples=200)],
    tracks=["retrieval"],
    pipeline=PipelineSweepSpec(
        base_profile="speed",
        rerankers=["cross_encoder", "my_ideas:keyword_overlap"],
    ),
    n_runs=1,
)
results = asyncio.run(Experiment(config).run())
for task in results.failed_tasks:
    print("failed:", task.task_key, task.error)
print(results.to_markdown("ndcg@10"))

Look at the failed tasks before the scores. A task that failed is listed there and not in the table.

docs.title: Sweep any stage
docs.text:
Five stages have a list key. The others are named in a config_overrides entry.

Stage How to sweep it reranker rerankers: [...] query enhancer query_enhancers: [...] chunker chunkers: [...] embedder embedders: [...] generator generators: [...] retriever config_overrides: [{name: bm25, retriever: bm25}] agentic pipeline config_overrides: [{name: ircot, agentic_pipeline: ircot}] document processor does not sweep; check it on your own files

An agentic pipeline arm changes generation metrics only, so sweep it with the generation track. A chunker or embedder arm gets a corpus of its own, chunked or embedded by its component, so arms never share an index. Every chunking or embedding setting (chunk_size, chunk_unit, embedding_model and so on) gets its own corpus in the same way.

docs.title: A retriever
docs.text:
Put dense, the default vector search as a component, in as the control. Then every arm names its first stage.

name: which first stage
benchmarks:
  - name: beir/scifact
    n_samples: 200
tracks: [retrieval]
pipeline:
  base_profile: speed
  config_overrides:
    - {name: dense, retriever: dense}           # the control
    - {name: bm25, retriever: bm25}
    - {name: hybrid_rrf, retriever: hybrid_rrf}
n_runs: 1

This one is keyless: BM25 needs no model, and speed embeds with the 92 MB one.

docs.title: A generator
docs.text:
List the answer strategies under generators:. Every arm retrieves the same way, so a difference comes from how the answer was written. concise is the harness's own prompt, word for word, so it is the control.

name: how the answer is written
benchmarks:
  - name: hotpotqa
    n_samples: 100
tracks: [generation]
pipeline:
  base_profile: speed
  generators: [concise, cited, chain_of_note]
n_runs: 3          # repeat runs when an LLM stage is in the loop

This one needs an LLM API key and the eval extra (see an LLM for the generation track). cited answers carry [n] markers, and the citation metrics score them. From the shell, lasagna benchmark run <name> --generator cited runs one generator.

docs.title: An ensemble of rerankers
docs.text:
ensemble averages the scores of the cross-encoders an arm names in ensemble_reranker_models. Weights go in ensemble_reranker_weights and are equal when left out. An arm with fewer than two models, or with one that cannot load, fails instead of scoring as one model.

pipeline:
  base_profile: speed
  config_overrides:
    - {name: minilm, reranker: cross_encoder}       # the control
    - name: ensemble
      reranker: ensemble
      ensemble_reranker_models: [cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2, cross-encoder/ms-marco-TinyBERT-L-2-v2]

mmr and combined (the cross-encoder followed by MMR) run MMR whatever enable_mmr says, because naming them is what turns it on.

docs.title: Live mode and pooled corpora
docs.text:
A component override is only measured in live mode. generation_only never constructs the pipeline, so passing reranker= there is a hard error rather than a plausible number scored from gold context. The default mode: auto picks the right mode and logs which it chose and why.

SQuAD v2, HotpotQA, MuSiQue and RAGBench ship each question's supporting passages inline and no corpus to search. In auto mode Lasagna pools those passages across every sample in the run, so each query has to find its own among all the others'. That is a real retrieval task, but an easier one: the pool holds no hard negatives, so recall reads higher than it would against a corpus of the same size. These runs are stamped corpus_provenance: pooled_gold, which is part of the comparability key, so a pooled number never shares a leaderboard row with a BEIR one. For the same questions against a real corpus, use beir/hotpotqa.

Natural Questions and TriviaQA carry no context at all and stay generation_only.

docs.title: How many runs
docs.text:
Retrieval with fixed models is deterministic. The same queries return the same ranked lists on every run, and the significance tests pair arms query by query, so n_runs: 1 gives the same answer as three runs, three times faster. A sweep that repeats identical runs says so when it ends.

Repeat runs when an LLM stage is in the loop: an answer generator, an LLM reranker, HyDE or an agentic pipeline. A model that takes no temperature (see temperature and repeatable runs) varies from run to run whatever you ask for. There, n_runs: 3 or more measures the spread, and variance_source: run keeps the queries fixed so the spread is run to run rather than a resampled subset.

docs.title: When corpus documents fail to ingest
docs.text:
A document that cannot be chunked (an error, or more than 120 s) is left out of the corpus, and the log names it. A partial corpus scores lower than the benchmark would, so every task on it fails, naming the count, the first documents and the setting that accepts it:

ingest_failure_tolerance: 0.02   # up to 2% of the corpus may be missing (at most 0.1)

A run that accepts a partial corpus records corpus_ingest_gap in each result. That is part of the comparability key, so the run never shares a leaderboard group with one on the complete corpus, and the bundle carries a PARTIAL_CORPUS warning.

docs.title: Read the verdict
docs.text:
lasagna results significance "<output>/results.json" -m ndcg@10 --all

The command prints each pair of arms with the difference, the effect size and both the raw and the Holm-adjusted p-value. It ends in a box. Green names each pair that survives the correction, which side won and by how much. Yellow says nothing survived and points at lasagna results power, which tells "the arms perform alike" apart from "too few queries to tell".

Question Command Is the gap real, across every pair of arms? lasagna results significance results.json --all Could this run have detected the effect I care about? lasagna results power results.json baseline candidate Do two techniques compose, or overlap? lasagna results interaction results.json (a 2x2 run) Which queries did an arm lose? lasagna results per-query results.json --sort-by ndcg@10 Are two runs comparable at all? lasagna results compare a.json b.json

Significance testing explains what the test does. Results, bundles and leaderboards covers sharing the run.

docs.title: Three more checks
docs.text: Dry run and cost estimates tells you what a sweep costs before it starts. Baselines adds the arms a reviewer asks for. The LLM response cache makes a second run of a sweep spend nothing on what it already asked.

docs.title: Dry run and cost estimates
docs.text: Check what a sweep will do before it spends time or tokens.

docs.title: Dry run
docs.text:
lasagna benchmark experiment sweep.yaml --dry-run              # with a 3-sample probe
lasagna benchmark experiment sweep.yaml --dry-run --no-probe   # nothing runs at all

A dry run prints the arms, the tasks, the models the run loads and whether each is already downloaded, and a token estimate. Unless you pass --no-probe, it runs three samples per benchmark and extrapolates tokens and time to the whole sweep. Every number is labeled an estimate, and nothing is written under the results folder.

For the plugin template's sweep it printed:

Arms (2): reranker=cross_encoder, reranker=template_length
Tasks (2): 1 benchmark x 2 arms x 1 run
  smoke  split=test  12 samples
Models:
  embedder           all-MiniLM-L6-v2  cached
  reranker           cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2  cached
  reranker           component template_length
Tokens: no generation track, so no answer is generated or judged; an arm still calls an LLM if its pipeline does (HyDE, an agentic pipeline, an LLM reranker).
Probe of smoke (estimate): arm 'reranker=cross_encoder' on 3 samples took 2.8 s including setup (loading models, ingesting), 0.12 s per query, 0 LLM calls
  Extrapolated to 24 queries (estimate, every arm assumed to spend what this one did): about 3 s of query time plus setup, 0 system tokens and 0 judge tokens

docs.title: Dollars, only if you ask
docs.text:
A run records tokens, which are observed. Add prices: to the sweep file for an estimate in dollars:

prices: builtin          # the dated table in the package (builtin-2026-10)
# or your own rates, in USD per million tokens, which win over the table:
# prices: {gpt-6-luna: {input_per_1m: 0.10, output_per_1m: 0.50}}

Each task whose tokens all have a rate gets cost_usd_estimate, and the run metadata records the table and the rates used. A rate that holds only for shorter prompts gives no estimate for a task whose calls average longer. With no prices:, a run reports tokens only.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The LLM response cache keeps a second run from paying again.

docs.title: Use LangChain or LlamaIndex components
docs.text:
lasagna.from_langchain and lasagna.from_llamaindex register an object you already have. Lasagna then compares it like any built-in component.

You have It becomes A LangChain document compressor, or a LlamaIndex node postprocessor A reranker Embeddings An embedder A retriever A retriever

The listing describes the entry as wrapped: langchain.<Class>.

import lasagna
from langchain_core.embeddings import DeterministicFakeEmbedding
from lasagna.core.registry import registry

name = lasagna.from_langchain(DeterministicFakeEmbedding(size=64))
print(name)  # langchain.DeterministicFakeEmbedding
entry = next(e for e in registry.list_embedders() if e["name"] == name)
print(entry["description"])  # wrapped: langchain.DeterministicFakeEmbedding

docs.title: Name it in a sweep
docs.text:
From Python, name the returned name like any other component.

A sweep file run with lasagna benchmark experiment names the object where you defined it instead. With cohere = CohereRerank(top_n=10) in my_rerankers.py, the arm "my_rerankers:cohere" is wrapped the same way:

name: Cohere against the cross-encoder
benchmarks:
  - name: beir/scifact
    n_samples: 200
tracks: [retrieval]
pipeline:
  base_profile: speed
  rerankers: [cross_encoder, "my_rerankers:cohere"]
n_runs: 1

docs.title: Three things to know
docs.text:
• A wrapped retriever brings its own index. It searches whatever the object was built over, not the corpus Lasagna ingested. For a benchmark, its index must hold that benchmark's corpus, with each corpus id in the metadata (doc_id, or the key you pass as id_key=). A document with no id gets a hash of its text, which matches no relevance judgment.
  • The object's own limits apply. A compressor's top_n or a retriever's k caps how many documents come back. Set it at least as high as the pipeline's depth, or the arm is scored on shorter lists than the others.
  • LlamaIndex is an extra. Install it with pip install "lasagna-rag[llamaindex]". LangChain needs nothing more.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• Compare a component runs the sweep.
  • Write a component covers components that are not wrapped.

docs.title: LLM response cache
docs.text:
Inside lasagna benchmark experiment, a request asked at temperature 0 that an earlier run made with the same seed is answered from ~/.lasagna/cache/llm.sqlite. A second run of the same sweep, after a crash or with one arm added, then spends no tokens on what it already asked.

Token counts read as in the cold run. llm_cache_hits and llm_cache_misses on each task, and a hit rate in results.json and the bundle, say what was replayed.

docs.title: What is never replayed
docs.text:
• Sampled calls. A response at temperature 0.7 is one draw. Replaying it would make repeated runs identical and hide the spread n_runs is meant to measure.
  • The RAGAS judge, which asks for temperature 0.01, unless you set llm_cache: {deterministic_only: false}.
  • Models that take no temperature. The cache replays a call only when temperature 0 was actually sent, so a model that gets no temperature (Claude 4.7 and later, some OpenAI reasoning models) is always called.

docs.title: Your own provider
docs.text: A provider you set with set_llm_provider gets the cache too. The chat model its get_chat_model returns is replayed when temperature 0 was asked for and the model's temperature is 0. A returned object that is not a LangChain chat model cannot carry the cache, and results.json then says "applied": false with the reason under llm_cache.

docs.title: Turn it off or move it
docs.text:
• llm_cache: false in the sweep file
  • --no-cache on the command
  • LASAGNA_LLM_CACHE=0 in the environment
  • llm_cache: {path: ...} puts the file elsewhere

Nothing is cached outside an experiment, so lasagna serve and the MCP server write no prompt to disk.

docs.title: Reproduce published BEIR numbers
docs.text: Lasagna's built-in retrievers and reranker reproduce published numbers on BEIR SciFact and NFCorpus. Both dense models land within 0.002 NDCG@10 of their MTEB results. BM25 followed by the MiniLM cross-encoder lands within 0.004 of the BEIR paper. No method was tuned. BM25 uses the k1 and b that BEIR used, and the dense models and the cross-encoder use their published checkpoints unchanged.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
NDCG@10 on the BEIR test splits: SciFact (300 queries, 5,183 documents) and NFCorpus (323 queries, 3,633 documents). The difference is Lasagna minus published.

Method Dataset Published Source Lasagna Difference BM25 (k1 0.9, b 0.4) SciFact 0.665 BEIR, Table 2 0.664 -0.001 BM25 (k1 0.9, b 0.4) NFCorpus 0.325 BEIR, Table 2 0.317 -0.008 all-MiniLM-L6-v2 SciFact 0.645 MTEB results 0.645 0.000 all-MiniLM-L6-v2 NFCorpus 0.316 MTEB results 0.317 +0.001 bge-small-en-v1.5 SciFact 0.713 MTEB results 0.713 0.000 bge-small-en-v1.5 NFCorpus 0.343 MTEB results 0.344 +0.001 BM25 + MiniLM-L6 cross-encoder SciFact 0.688 BEIR, Table 2 0.685 -0.003 BM25 + MiniLM-L6 cross-encoder NFCorpus 0.350 BEIR, Table 2 0.351 +0.001

The BM25 rows sit slightly below the BEIR paper because the paper indexed the title and the text as separate fields, and Lasagna indexes one field. Against the single-field Anserini runs, BM25 is 0.015 (SciFact) and 0.005 (NFCorpus) below. The reproduction README has the Recall@100 tables, the arms with no published target, and the notes on each difference.

results.csv has every measured number to four decimals. It also records the query count and where the numbers come from: the run date, the package and metrics versions, and the commit.

docs.title: Rerun it
docs.text:
From a clone of the repository:

pip install "lasagna-rag[eval]"
python -m nltk.downloader punkt_tab
lasagna benchmark experiment examples/reproduction/beir_tier1.yaml

To compare your run with these numbers, write its own results.csv and diff the measured columns (the first seven). No output means they match:

python examples/reproduction/results_csv.py "<the Output folder the run printed>" > mine.csv
diff <(cut -d, -f1-7 examples/reproduction/results.csv) <(cut -d, -f1-7 mine.csv)

The sweep needs no LLM and no API key. The first run downloads the two datasets (about 15 MB) and three models (about 300 MB). The sweep is 28 tasks, 14 arms on each dataset. On an Apple M1 Max it took 31 minutes with the models and datasets already downloaded, and 37 minutes on a first run.

Every arm is deterministic, so the sweep runs once (n_runs: 1). Three runs, each from an empty store, gave identical results.

docs.title: What the sweep holds fixed
docs.text:
Every arm starts from the speed profile. An arm then names one first stage (retriever: bm25, dense or hybrid_rrf) and, in the cross-encoder arm, one reranker. Nothing else differs between arms.

  • Whole documents. BEIR scores documents, and the harness retrieves chunks. The sweep makes each document exactly one chunk, so no document is cut.
  • Truncation at the model's limit. all-MiniLM-L6-v2 reads the first 256 tokens of a document. bge-small-en-v1.5 and the cross-encoder read the first 512, as in the published setups.
  • Query instruction. bge-small-en-v1.5 queries get the instruction from its model card, which MTEB also applies. all-MiniLM-L6-v2 takes none.
  • Rerank depth. The cross-encoder reorders the BM25 top 100.
  • Scoring. NDCG@10 uses linear gain, as trec_eval does. Rescoring every ranked list with pytrec_eval, the evaluator BEIR uses, gave the same numbers to four decimals.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• BEIR: Thakur, Reimers, Rücklé, Srivastava and Gurevych, "BEIR: A Heterogeneous Benchmark for Zero-shot Evaluation of Information Retrieval Models", NeurIPS 2021 Datasets and Benchmarks Track, arXiv:2104.08663v4.
  • MTEB results: embeddings-benchmark/results.
  • Anserini and Pyserini: the Pyserini BEIR regressions.

docs.title: Read and publish results
docs.text: Every run writes a results.json and prints its path. Each command on this page takes it.

docs.title: Answer a question about the run
docs.text:
Question Command Is the gap real, across every pair of arms? lasagna results significance results.json --all Could this run have detected the effect I care about? lasagna results power results.json baseline candidate Do two techniques compose, or overlap? lasagna results interaction results.json (a 2x2 run) Which queries did an arm lose, at retrieval or generation? lasagna results per-query results.json --sort-by ndcg@10 Are two runs comparable at all? lasagna results compare a.json b.json

significance runs a paired sign-flip test on every pair of arms and corrects the p-values with Holm-Bonferroni. It ends in a box that says what the table supports. Green names each pair that survives and which side won. Yellow says nothing survived and points at power. The significance concept page explains the method.

docs.title: Share the whole run as one page
docs.text:
lasagna results view results.json -o view.html

The page carries the versions and run id, the stage isolation check, and, for each benchmark, the leaderboard, the significance table with its verdict, every metric per arm, and a per-query diff between two arms. Use --diff A B to pick the arms. The default is the top two. Each diff shows what each arm retrieved.

It is one file with no external requests. It opens offline, and you can attach it to a review.

docs.title: Put a leaderboard in a paper
docs.text:
mkdir -p bundles
lasagna results bundle results.json -o bundles/run.json
lasagna results leaderboard bundles/ --format latex

--format latex prints one booktabs table for each comparability group. Rows in one table held the same configuration fixed. Rows in different tables are never ranked together. With -o, it writes one .tex file per benchmark instead. Arm names are escaped for LaTeX.

Every results command that reads a bundle checks it as results validate does. A bundle that fails is refused with its problems listed, or left out of a folder's leaderboard with its name printed. A failure means a number was edited after the bundle was made, or provenance is missing. --allow-invalid on leaderboard and view shows the bundle anyway, with every number marked INVALID. A results.json is not a bundle, and is shown as not validated.

docs.title: Publish a number someone else can check
docs.text:
lasagna results bundle results.json -o run.json
lasagna results validate run.json

The bundle carries the library versions, the hardware, the resolved sweep, the corpus fingerprint and the comparability key. validate recomputes the key, the run id and every aggregate from the per-query scores.

It also lists integrity warnings that do not invalidate a bundle:

  • SINGLE_RUN: one run of a pipeline in which something samples.
  • UNRESOLVED_JUDGE_ALIAS: a judge named by a floating alias.
  • PARTIAL_CORPUS: some corpus documents failed to ingest.

--strict turns the warnings into failures. A run records nothing_samples when only retrieval ran and no task called an LLM. One run of it is complete and raises no SINGLE_RUN.

See comparability and provenance for what the key holds fixed. The results schema lists every field.

docs.title: The results hub
docs.text: The results hub runs a public leaderboard from bundles. A submission is a pull request that adds one JSON file. The hub marks a row verified only when someone else's bundle reproduces it: within its spread, which needs at least two runs, or by equalling its mean when nothing in the run samples.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Command What it does lasagna results significance Test every pair of arms. lasagna results power Estimate whether the run could detect an effect. lasagna results interaction Test whether two techniques compose. lasagna results per-query List the queries an arm lost. lasagna results compare Check whether two runs are comparable. lasagna results view Write a one-file HTML report. lasagna results bundle Package a run with its provenance. lasagna results validate Re-check a bundle. lasagna results leaderboard Build leaderboards from bundles. lasagna results schema Print the bundle schema.

Every option is in the CLI reference.

docs.title: Make a development set from your documents
docs.text:
Use this when you have documents but no questions. Lasagna asks an LLM to write questions from your files, checks each one, and saves them in the JSONL format that benchmark run and benchmark experiment read.

For development, not for claims

Scores on a synthetic set read high. See Synthetic sets are for development, not for claims.

docs.title: Plan first
docs.text:
lasagna benchmark synthesize ./docs --n 200 --out my_bench.jsonl \
    --mix factoid=0.6,multihop=0.3,unanswerable=0.1 --seed 42 --dry-run

--dry-run prints the plan (documents, passages, questions of each type, LLM calls) and a token estimate. It calls no LLM and writes nothing.

docs.title: Generate
docs.text:
Drop --dry-run and set an API key such as OPENAI_API_KEY or ANTHROPIC_API_KEY. Use MODEL_NAME or --model to choose the model.

The command reads every supported file under the folder (.md and .txt as plain text, PDF, DOCX and HTML through the same extractor as an upload). It cuts each file into 200-word passages with the fixed chunker, then asks for three kinds of question:

Type What it asks factoid A short fact found in one passage. multihop A fact from each of two passages in two different documents. unanswerable A question on the subject of a passage that the passage does not answer.

A second call checks each question. Rows that fail are dropped and counted, so the file can hold fewer than --n rows. The summary says how many and why.

The same folder, seed and model give the same plan and the same prompts.

docs.title: Score one question type
docs.text:
Each row records how it was made, including question_type. To score one type, filter on it in the benchmark entry of a sweep:

name: Synthetic multihop
benchmarks:
  - path: my_bench.jsonl
    filters: {question_type: multihop}
pipeline:
  base_profile: speed
  rerankers: [cross_encoder, mmr]
n_runs: 1

docs.title: From Python
docs.text:
from lasagna.knowledge_evaluation_sdk.synthesize import synthesize, write_jsonl

rows = synthesize("docs", n=200, mix="factoid=0.6,multihop=0.3,unanswerable=0.1", seed=42)
write_jsonl(rows, "my_bench.jsonl")

docs.title: Choose a vector backend
docs.text: Lasagna stores and searches chunk embeddings through one interface, VectorStoreAdapter. Six backends implement it: Milvus, Qdrant, Pinecone, Weaviate, PgVector and OpenSearch. You pick one with the vector_backend setting. The rest of the pipeline does not change.

docs.title: Install the client
docs.text:
Milvus, with Milvus Lite, ships with the core package. The others need their client library through an extra. Without it, get_backend(name) raises ValueError and names the extra to install.

Backend Install Read from the environment when no arguments are given milvus core MILVUS_URI, MILVUS_TOKEN. Otherwise Milvus Lite at <db dir>/rag_milvus.db. qdrant pip install "lasagna-rag[vector-backends]" QDRANT_URL, QDRANT_API_KEY. Otherwise local files in <db dir>/qdrant_data. pinecone pip install "lasagna-rag[vector-backends]" PINECONE_API_KEY weaviate pip install "lasagna-rag[vector-backends]" WEAVIATE_URL, WEAVIATE_API_KEY. Otherwise embedded Weaviate. pgvector pip install "lasagna-rag[pgvector]" PGVECTOR_DSN, then RAG_DATABASE_DSN. Otherwise postgresql://rag:rag@localhost:5432/rag. opensearch pip install "lasagna-rag[opensearch]" OPENSEARCH_HOSTS (default http://localhost:9200), OPENSEARCH_USER, OPENSEARCH_PASSWORD, OPENSEARCH_USE_SSL, OPENSEARCH_VERIFY_CERTS, OPENSEARCH_TIMEOUT

<db dir> is ~/.lasagna/dbs unless LASAGNA_DB_DIR or LASAGNA_DATA_DIR says otherwise.

To run a backend in containers, see Docker and Compose.

docs.title: Select it
docs.text:
Where How Environment LASAGNA_VECTOR_BACKEND=qdrant (or RAG_VECTOR_BACKEND) Settings file vector_backend = "qdrant" in the [rag] section of settings.lasagna.toml SDK KnowledgeConfig(vector_backend="qdrant", vector_backend_config={"url": "http://localhost:6333"}) One session, over REST PATCH /api/v1/config with {"vector_backend": "qdrant"} and the session's X-Session-ID header Setup lasagna init asks for one and writes a local configuration file

vector_backend_config (or LASAGNA_VECTOR_BACKEND_CONFIG as a JSON object) holds the constructor arguments. When it is empty, the backend reads the environment variables in the table above. The process-wide backend is built once, at startup, so changing either setting later needs a restart.

Switching moves no data

Documents indexed in the previous backend stay there. Each document row records its vector_backend_name and collection_name, and deleting the document deletes its vectors from that backend and collection.

Every setting is in the settings reference.

docs.title: Constructor arguments
docs.text:
get_backend(name, **kwargs) passes kwargs to the backend's constructor.

from lasagna.vector_backends import get_backend

get_backend("milvus", db_path="/data/milvus.db")                     # Milvus Lite
get_backend("milvus", uri="http://localhost:19530", token="...")     # Milvus server or Zilliz Cloud
get_backend("qdrant", path="/data/qdrant")                           # local files
get_backend("qdrant", url="https://...", api_key="...")              # server or Qdrant Cloud
get_backend("pinecone", api_key="...", cloud="aws", region="us-east-1")
get_backend("weaviate", embedded=True)
get_backend("weaviate", url="https://...", api_key="...")            # an api_key means Weaviate Cloud
get_backend("pgvector", dsn="postgresql://rag:rag@localhost:5432/rag", pool_min=2, pool_max=10)
get_backend("opensearch", hosts=["https://search.example.com:9200"],
            http_auth=("user", "pass"), use_ssl=True, language="german")

A db_path together with a server address stops startup with a ConfigError that names both.

docs.title: Collections: one per embedding model
docs.text:
The default collection name is rag_documents_v2__<model>__<dim>. The default model, BAAI/bge-m3 at 1024 dimensions, writes to rag_documents_v2__baai_bge_m3__1024.

Opening an existing collection with another model, or at another dimension, raises CollectionIdentityError, which names the command that switches back. Nothing is dropped, except an empty collection at the wrong dimension, which is rebuilt. One collection per embedding model explains what this means when you change models.

docs.title: What each backend supports
docs.text:
Milvus Lite Milvus server Qdrant Pinecone Weaviate PgVector OpenSearch Native hybrid search no yes no no yes yes yes Native BM25 no yes no no yes no yes Partitions or namespaces yes yes no yes no no no Dynamic schema yes yes yes yes yes no yes Max batch size 1000 1000 1000 100 1000 5000 10000 Max vector dimension 32768 32768 65536 20000 65536 16000 16000

Without native hybrid search, the pipeline fuses dense results with an in-process BM25 index when enable_hybrid_search is on.

Scores are normalized for most backends, and OpenSearch returns its own. Compare scores within one backend, not across backends.

docs.title: Filters
docs.text:
FilterExpression is written once and translated for each backend.

from lasagna.vector_backends import FilterExpression

FilterExpression.eq("session_id", "s1")          # also ne, gt, gte, lt, lte
FilterExpression.in_list("document_id", ["d1", "d2"])   # also not_in_list
FilterExpression.like("content", "%heart%")
FilterExpression.prefix("document_id", "doc_")
FilterExpression.json_eq("metadata", "source", "pubmed")

expr = (FilterExpression.eq("session_id", "s1") & FilterExpression.gte("page", 2)) | FilterExpression.eq("pinned", True)
negated = ~FilterExpression.eq("archived", True)

An operator a backend cannot express raises UnsupportedFilterError naming the operator and the backend. It is never dropped.

docs.title: Add your own backend
docs.text:
Subclass VectorStoreAdapter, implement its abstract members, and register it:

from lasagna.vector_backends import VectorStoreAdapter, get_backend, register_backend


class ChromaBackend(VectorStoreAdapter):
    ...  # backend_name, capabilities and the abstract methods


register_backend("chroma", ChromaBackend)
backend = get_backend("chroma")

The vector backends README lists the members to implement, with a runnable round trip.

tests/test_vector_backend_conformance.py asserts one contract against every backend it can reach: collections, insert and search, filters, delete, paging and declared capabilities. Run it against yours to find out where it differs.

docs.title: API
docs.text: VectorStoreAdapter and register_backend are documented in the Python API reference.

docs.title: Write a component
docs.text:
A component fills one stage of the pipeline. Lasagna has eight stages, and you can write a component for each one. The path has five steps, and each one is a checkpoint that can fail:

# Step Command 1 Write it one decorator on a function 2 Check the contract lasagna component validate my_ideas:keyword_overlap 3 Check it runs lasagna benchmark run smoke --reranker my_ideas:keyword_overlap --profile speed 4 Check it helps lasagna benchmark experiment sweep.yaml 5 Publish lasagna results bundle, then validate

Contributing a component explains each step and what it rules out. This page is the short version for writing the code.

docs.title: A function per stage
docs.text:
Most techniques fit in one function. The decorator @lasagna.<stage> wraps the function in the stage's interface and registers it. The wrapper hands your function copies of what it receives, so it cannot change what another stage sees.

Stage Decorator Function reranker @lasagna.reranker f(query, text) -> float, or f(query, documents, top_k) -> documents query enhancer @lasagna.query_enhancer f(query) -> list[str] chunker @lasagna.chunker f(text) -> list[str] embedder @lasagna.embedder f(texts) -> one vector per text retriever @lasagna.retriever f(query, top_k) -> list[str] or documents document processor @lasagna.document_processor f(file_path) -> str generator @lasagna.generator f(query, contexts) -> str 
import lasagna

@lasagna.reranker(
    "keyword_overlap", paper="Someone et al. 2026", claims={"beir/scifact": {"ndcg@10": 0.42}}
)
def keyword_overlap(query, text):
    """Count the query words that appear in the passage."""
    return len(set(query.lower().split()) & set(text.lower().split()))

The agentic pipeline is the one stage with no one-line form, because a loop is a class.

docs.title: A class when you have state
docs.text:
A technique with state or a model is a class. Subclass the stage's interface (BaseReranker, BaseAgenticPipeline and so on from lasagna.core.base_components), register it with @registry.register("reranker", "name"), and copy your inputs before you change them.

Registration and conformance are different things. A class can register and still not satisfy its interface. It is then listed with implements_contract: False, and comparing against it measures the interface difference along with the algorithm. This lists the fair baselines:

from lasagna.core.registry import registry

[r["name"] for r in registry.list_rerankers() if r["implements_contract"]]

docs.title: Record the paper and the claim
docs.text:
paper and claims are optional, and they are worth filling in. They come back out of the registry, and a run records them. On a run of the benchmark a claim names, the leaderboards and lasagna results view show the claimed number beside the one you reproduced.

A claim is keyed by benchmark, {"beir/scifact": {"ndcg@10": 0.42}}, with "split": "test" inside if the paper names a split. Three rules apply:

  • A claim that names no benchmark is refused, because it would print beside a run of any benchmark.
  • A bad metric name is refused when you register.
  • An unknown benchmark is a warning that names the closest one.

docs.title: Check the contract
docs.text:
lasagna component validate my_ideas:keyword_overlap

The command imports from the working directory, as a sweep does. It checks the return types, top_k, empty input and that the component does not change its input. A plain function with no decorator needs --stage <stage>. A class is named my_package.reranker:MyReranker.

A green result does not mean the pipeline can call your component, because the check runs the component alone. Step 3, lasagna benchmark run smoke, runs it inside the pipeline.

docs.title: Share it as a package
docs.text: To publish a component as an installable package, start from the plugin template. lasagna plugins list shows installed plugins and names any that failed to load. For a new kind of component, not just a new implementation, see Extending.

docs.title: Publish the bundle with your number
docs.text:
If you report a number from the evaluation harness, publish its results bundle with it:

lasagna results bundle results.json -o run.json

The bundle carries what a reader needs to decide whether your number and theirs measure the same thing. See comparability and provenance.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: The most useful contributions are new components to compare: a reranker, chunker, query enhancer or agentic pipeline. Changes to the core are welcome too.

docs.title: Set up
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna && cd lasagna
uv pip install -e ".[all]" --group dev
pre-commit install
pytest tests/ --ignore=tests/live --ignore=tests/stress

The suite keeps the Hugging Face hub offline and downloads nothing. A test that needs weights you have not cached skips and names them.

docs.title: Add a component
docs.text: Read write a component for the short path, and contributing components for the full contract, the conformance checks and the pull request checklist.

docs.title: Build these docs
docs.text:
The docs use MkDocs. Install the pinned toolchain and build in strict mode, which fails on any broken link:

pip install --group docs
mkdocs build --strict
mkdocs serve

Three pages are generated from the code: the CLI reference, the catalog and the settings reference. Do not edit them by hand. Each has a script in scripts/ and a test that fails when the page is stale. Every lasagna ... command in a docs code block is checked against the real command line.

docs.title: Find something to work on
docs.text: Wanted lists the components, benchmarks and studies the project would like to have, each with what "done" means. Comment on an item's issue to claim it.

docs.title: The bar for a pull request
docs.text:
Every pull request is read in full by a person who will maintain it, so the bar is the same whoever or whatever wrote the code. A check runs on every pull request and fails until:

  • the description fills in the template: why, what changed, how it was tested, the evidence, and which agent was used, if any;
  • a person names themselves, by GitHub handle, as having read every line of the diff;
  • every suppression in the lines added names its code and gives a reason, and every TODO links its issue;
  • a change to src/lasagna/ comes with a test and a changelog line.

Run it before you open the pull request:

python scripts/check_pr_body.py --file body.md --diff origin/main

AI coding agents are welcome under the same bar. A pull request below it is closed with a link to the quality bar, and can be opened again once it meets it.

docs.title: The rest
docs.text: The contributing guide covers the definition of done for each kind of change, bug reports and how to disagree about a number. The code of conduct applies to every space.

docs.title: Governance
docs.text: Lasagna has one maintainer today, Ido Levy (@dolev31), who has the final say on what merges. That describes where the project is. It is not a permanent structure. If a second person reviews regularly and their judgment is good, they get commit rights, and the governance file changes.

docs.title: Correctness is settled by evidence
docs.text: Deciding what merges does not decide what is true. If you can show that a metric, a statistic or a benchmark adapter is wrong, that ends the argument, whoever wrote it. The bar is a failing test or a reproducible demonstration.

docs.title: Result disputes
docs.text:
If you think a published result is wrong, open a result dispute on GitHub. Most resolve with one command:

lasagna results compare theirs.json yours.json

The field-level diff usually shows that the two runs held different things fixed. The comparability key exists for this.

Read the full governance file.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: Report vulnerabilities privately through GitHub Security Advisories. Do not open a public issue. The project aims to acknowledge a report within three working days.

docs.title: What to know before you serve
docs.text:
• The REST API is unauthenticated by default. It is meant for a trusted network. In that mode, X-Session-ID is accepted as identity with no credential, so anything that can reach the port can read or delete any session's documents. Turn on RAG_REQUIRE_AUTH before you publish it. See REST API.
  • No default credentials. Every credential is required configuration.
  • A session cannot reconfigure the server. The settings a session may set for itself are retrieval and generation settings. The vector backend, its connection settings, paths, URLs, credentials and server limits come from the environment and the settings file only.
  • The MCP server has two tool sets. The safe set leaves out the tools that delete or reconfigure. See MCP server.

Read the full security policy.

docs.title: Wanted
docs.text:
What Lasagna would like to have next, and what "done" means for each. Every item has an open issue; comment there to claim it.

A method in Lasagna is measured against every other component of its stage, in a complete pipeline, on the same benchmarks, with everything else held fixed. If your paper's method is here, anyone can check it against theirs with one sweep, and the catalog lists it beside its paper.

If you want to Start with Add your paper's method Components Make a first pull request Good first issues Add a dataset Benchmarks Run a study Research questions Run Lasagna in production Deployment

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
Written for authors of RAG methods. The path is six commands, and contributing components walks through each: write the component, lasagna component validate, a smoke run, a sweep against a built-in control, lasagna results significance, then lasagna results bundle. The worked example there is a toy reranker against cross_encoder on 100 SciFact queries: cross_encoder wins by +0.0913 ndcg@10 (d_z +0.38, p (Holm) 1.0e-04).

Stage Method Paper Note document_processor Unstructured repository No paper. Layout-aware parsing for mixed files. embedder jina-embeddings-v2, with late chunking 2409.04701 Late chunking exists as a setting; this is the Jina embedder behind it. retriever RAPTOR 2401.18059 The tree code exists behind enable_raptor; it needs registering as a retriever. retriever GraphRAG, LightRAG, HippoRAG, G-Retriever 2404.16130, 2410.05779, 2405.14831, 2402.07630 A small graph retriever exists behind enable_graph_retrieval; register it first. retriever ColBERTv2 with PLAID 2112.01488 Late interaction as a retriever, with its own index. retriever ColPali 2407.01449 Page images as the documents. reranker RankZephyr, RankVicuna 2312.02724, 2309.15088 Open-weight listwise rerankers, beside the built-in llm_listwise. reranker Setwise 2310.09497 Fewer LLM calls than listwise. agentic_pipeline Search-o1, Search-R1 2501.05366, 2503.09516 A model that reasons and issues its own searches. none yet RECOMP, LongLLMLingua 2310.04408, 2310.06839 Context compression has no stage. Post a short design first: which stage, and what it returns.

Already in Lasagna, so not on this list: BGE-M3, the ColBERT reranker, llm_listwise, self_ask, ircot, MarkItDown, PyMuPDF4LLM, OpenTelemetry tracing, and local models through Ollama, vLLM, Hugging Face and llama.cpp. The component catalog lists all 55.

Done when:

  • the component is registered with paper=, and with claims= when the paper reports a number on a benchmark Lasagna runs, so every leaderboard prints the paper's number beside yours;
  • lasagna component validate passes;
  • any weights it downloads are listed in src/lasagna/core/model_licenses.py;
  • a results bundle compares it with a built-in control of its stage, at n_runs: 1 when only retrieval is measured and 3 or more with an LLM in the loop;
  • it ships in Lasagna through a pull request that meets the pull request checklist, or as a package of your own with a lasagna_components entry point (template). Both count; a package of your own needs no review from us.

Your method is not in the table? Propose it with the component form. Open items are labeled component-wanted.

docs.title: Good first issues
docs.text:
Small, with the files named and a test to write. Labeled good first issue.

  • Claims for the built-in components. A component can declare the number its paper reports; no built-in declares one yet. Each one filled in puts a published number beside a reproduced one.
  • A benchmark adapter. MIRACL and BRIGHT, below.

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text:
Every built-in benchmark loads at a pinned revision, states its license and is listed in DATASETS.md. Propose one with the benchmark form; open items are labeled benchmark.

Benchmark Paper Why MIRACL 2210.09984 Lasagna's benchmarks are English. MIRACL has human-judged relevance in 18 languages; start with one. BRIGHT 2407.12883 Relevance that needs reasoning, not word overlap. Shows whether a reranker or query enhancer helps when matching is not enough.

To evaluate on data of your own, no adapter is needed: see your own data.

docs.title: Research questions
docs.text:
Open questions that Lasagna can answer with a sweep. Write the plan before the run (the question, what changes, what is held fixed, and the result that would prove you wrong) with the research form. Either answer is worth publishing. Labeled research.

  • Does composition hold with an open-weight generator? The paper tests whether the effect of changing one stage depends on the others, and every answer in it comes from one proprietary model, GPT-5.1.
  • How much of the scaling loss survives out-of-domain distractors? The paper grows the corpus with distractors drawn from the same five domains as the corpus, and calls the result directional rather than a scaling law. Real corpora often grow with documents from other domains.
  • How well does the judge agree with people? Faithfulness is scored by an LLM judge, and Lasagna does not yet measure that judge against human labels.

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text:
For people running Lasagna as a service. Labeled deployment.

  • Vector backends: Chroma, LanceDB, Elasticsearch. Six run today. Each new one is an adapter class and the shared conformance test, which says where an adapter differs. See vector backends.
  • An OpenAI-compatible answer endpoint, with streaming. The REST API searches, but has no route that retrieves and then answers, and nothing streams.
  • Weights & Biases and MLflow. A run writes a results bundle; nothing sends it to a tracker yet.

Also planned for 0.2.0, with no issue yet: export and import of a session's documents and chunks, a prebuilt Wikipedia index, and batched generation with vLLM. Open an issue before you start one.

docs.title: How to claim an item
docs.text:
1. Comment on its issue: "I'm taking this."
  2. Open a draft pull request within two weeks, or the claim lapses and someone else can take it.
  3. Before you ask for review, meet the bar.

Questions go to Discussions.

Generated by scripts/gen_cli_doc.py from the Typer app in src/lasagna/cli.py. Do not edit by hand: run the script.

Every command is lasagna <command> [options]. lasagna <command> --help prints the same text in your terminal. Commands are grouped by what they work on:

Group Commands What it is for Documents export, import, init, search, status, upload Put documents into a session and search them. Benchmarks benchmark experiment, benchmark info, benchmark licenses, benchmark list, benchmark run, benchmark synthesize, benchmark validate-data Run benchmarks and sweeps, and read what they say about your change. Results results bundle, results compare, results interaction, results leaderboard, results per-query, results power, results schema, results significance, results validate, results view Read, compare, test and publish what a run wrote. Components component list, component validate List the components that fill each stage, and check one of yours. Plugins plugins list See which installed packages add components or benchmarks. Pipelines pipelines list See the agentic RAG pipelines you can select. Skills skills install, skills list Install the agent skill that teaches a coding agent to use Lasagna. Setup and serving configure, doctor, serve Set up, configure, diagnose and serve.

Options that apply before any command:

Option Description --verbose, -v Show INFO and DEBUG logs (default: warnings only) --version Print the installed version and exit. --install-completion, --show-completion Install shell completion, or print it to copy.

$ lasagna init

Interactive setup wizard for RAG knowledge base.

Asks for a vector backend and a quality profile, writes the backend to ./settings.lasagna.toml and applies the profile to the default session. The profile decides the embedding model. The LLM provider is not asked for: Lasagna picks it from the API key exported in the shell, so init names the provider that key selects, or which variable to export. API keys are not asked for or written anywhere.

$ lasagna results compare [OPTIONS] A B

Compare two runs, reporting whether they are comparable at all.

Each side is a run's results.json (or its folder) or a bundle. A bundle is checked first, as results validate checks it, and one that fails is refused. Per benchmark, configs are comparable when their comparability keys match: the keys results bundle prints and the leaderboard groups by.

docs.title: lasagna results interaction
docs.text:
$ lasagna results interaction [OPTIONS] RESULTS_PATH

Do two techniques compose, or do they overlap?

Estimates (AB - neither) - (A - neither) - (B - neither) from a 2x2 run. The p-value is a paired sign-flip permutation test on each query's interaction, and the confidence interval a t interval. A is reported against a baseline, B is reported against a baseline, and whether A+B is worth A alone cannot be recovered from the two, because the interaction is not a function of the main effects.

Arguments

Argument Required Description RESULTS_PATH yes results.json from a factorial run

Options

Option Type Default Description --benchmark str Which benchmark (default: the only one) --metric, -m str ndcg@10 Metric to test. --neither str neither Config with both techniques off --only-a str Config with technique A only --only-b str Config with technique B only --both str Config with both on --alpha float 0.05 Significance level of the test. --resamples int 10000 Random sign patterns for the sign-flip permutation test when more than 30 queries differ; with 30 or fewer it is exact. The interval is a t interval. --bootstrap int Old name of --resamples, removed in 0.2.0.

docs.title: lasagna results leaderboard
docs.text:
$ lasagna results leaderboard [OPTIONS] DIRECTORY

Leaderboards of bundles or a run's results.json, by comparability key.

Rows inside a group held the same configuration fixed, so they are comparable by construction. Rows in different groups are not, and are never put in the same table. A results.json with no --output prints the run's own leaderboard, the one benchmark experiment prints when it finishes. Bundles are checked as results validate checks them: one that fails is refused when named on its own and left out of a folder, unless --allow-invalid shows it marked INVALID. A results.json is not validated.

Arguments

Argument Required Description DIRECTORY yes A directory of validated bundles, one bundle, or a run's results.json (or its folder)

Options

Option Type Default Description --metric, -m str ndcg@10 Metric to rank by. --output, -o str Folder to write one page per benchmark into (.md, or .tex with --format latex), plus index.json --format str markdown markdown, or latex: one booktabs table per comparability group, printed when no --output is given --allow-invalid off Show bundles results validate rejects, each number marked INVALID

docs.title: lasagna results per-query
docs.text:
$ lasagna results per-query [OPTIONS] RESULTS_PATH

One row per query, retrieval and generation metrics side by side.

Turns "config A lost" into "config A lost on the multi-hop questions, at retrieval rather than generation".

In the JSONL export, _retrieved lists each document's score and rank. The rank is authoritative: scores can tie, so sorting by score does not rebuild the ranking the metrics were computed on.

Arguments

Argument Required Description RESULTS_PATH yes results.json from a run

Options

Option Type Default Description --output, -o str Write to .csv or .jsonl --benchmark str Restrict to one benchmark --config str Restrict to one config --limit int 20 Rows to print when not writing a file --sort-by str Metric to sort ascending (worst first)

docs.title: lasagna results power
docs.text:
$ lasagna results power [OPTIONS] RESULTS_PATH CONFIG_A CONFIG_B

Could this run have detected the effect you care about?

A non-significant result has two readings: the techniques are the same, or the run was too small to tell. They call for opposite next steps. Reports the smallest difference this run could have detected, and how many queries the observed difference would need.

Arguments

Argument Required Description RESULTS_PATH yes results.json from a run CONFIG_A yes Baseline config CONFIG_B yes Candidate config

Options

Option Type Default Description --metric, -m str ndcg@10 Metric to test. --benchmark str Which benchmark --alpha float 0.05 Significance level of the test. --power float 0.8 Chance of detecting the effect, for the smallest one reported.
